sections.title: Random experiments and the sample space

board_events.text: What is a RANDOM EXPERIMENT?
An action whose result you cannot predict, but whose full list of possible results you CAN list in advance.
$2+3=5$ is NOT random — there is no uncertainty in the result.
Each single result on the menu = an OUTCOME (a sample point).
The complete menu of all outcomes = the SAMPLE SPACE, written $S$.

segments.text: <curious>Here's the big idea.</curious> Any action whose result you cannot predict, yet whose complete list of possible results you can write down beforehand, is a random experiment.

Picture standing at a railway counter waiting to hear your berth. You don't know which one you'll get, but you know the whole menu in advance. Tossing a coin, rolling a die, drawing a card, all random experiments.

The word random is doing real work. Add two plus three and you always get five, no uncertainty, so nothing random. You need genuine doubt about the result but total clarity about the list of candidates.
Each single result sitting on that menu is called an outcome, or a sample point. Roll the die and land on a four, that four is one outcome.
Collect every outcome into one set and you get the sample space, written capital S. S is the universe of the experiment, everything else we discuss lives inside it.
For a single die, S contains one, two, three, four, five and six, so n of S equals six.
For one coin, S is just Heads and Tails, so n of S equals two.
Picture the die's sample space as six little cards laid on the table. That full spread of six cards is S. Hold this image, because the very next idea is built right on top of it.
यह है big idea। कोई भी action जिसका result आप पहले से predict नहीं कर सकते, फिर भी जिसके saare possible results आप पहले से लिख सकते हो — उसे random experiment कहते हैं।
सोचो आप railway counter पर खड़े हो, अपनी berth का wait कर रहे हो। आपको पता नहीं कौन सी मिलेगी, पर पूरा menu पहले से पता है। Coin toss, die roll, card draw — ये सब random experiments हैं।
यहाँ random word बहुत important है। Two plus three करोगे तो हमेशा five आएगा, कोई uncertainty नहीं, तो कुछ random नहीं। Result में genuine doubt चाहिए, पर list बिल्कुल clear।
उस menu पर बैठा हर single result एक outcome कहलाता है, या sample point। Die roll करके four आया, तो वो four एक outcome है।
अब saare outcomes को एक set में इकट्ठा करो, तो बनता है sample space, capital S। S इस experiment का universe है, बाक़ी सब कुछ इसी के अंदर रहता है।
एक die के लिए, S में होते हैं one, two, three, four, five और six, तो n of S equals six।
एक coin के लिए, S सिर्फ़ Heads और Tails है, तो n of S equals two।
<curious>Die के sample space को ऐसे सोचो जैसे table पर छह little cards रखी हों।</curious> छह cards का यह पूरा spread ही S है। इस image को पकड़ के रखो, क्योंकि अगला idea इसी पर खड़ा है।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: Events as subsets of S

board_events.text: An EVENT is a subset of S
Lay the six faces out as cards. An event = you scooping up the cards you care about.
"Even number" scoops up {2,4,6}. "Bigger than 4" scoops up {5,6}.
Event = subset. The single most important sentence in this subtopic.
An event OCCURS if the actual outcome is one of the cards you scooped.
Roll a 4: even occurred, since $4 \in \{2,4,6\}$. Roll a 3: it did not, since $3 \notin \{2,4,6\}$.

segments.text: Here is the single most important idea in this whole subtopic. An event is nothing more than a subset of the sample space.
Take those six die faces and lay them out as six cards. An event is just you reaching in and scooping up the cards you care about, any selection you like.
Say you care about even numbers, you scoop up two, four and six. Care about numbers bigger than four, you scoop up five and six. That's all it is.
So the event even is the set two, four, six, and the event bigger than four is the set five, six. Both are subsets of S.
<excited>Burn this into memory: event equals subset.</excited> Once you see events as subsets, every rule later is just set theory you already know from Chapter one.
When has an event occurred? Simple. An event occurs if the actual outcome you got is one of the cards you scooped up.
Roll a four, your even event occurred, because four is inside the set two, four, six. Roll a three, it did not, because three is not in that set.
In the picture, S is the whole box and A is the circle inside it holding two, four and six. The one, three and five sit in S but outside A, they're outcomes your event simply didn't scoop.
<excited>यह इस पूरे subtopic का सबसे important idea है!</excited> एक event sample space के एक subset से ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं है।
उन छह die faces को छह cards की तरह रखो। Event बस यह है कि आप उनमें से जो cards चाहो उठा लो, कोई भी selection।
मान लो आपको even numbers चाहिए, तो आप two, four और six उठाते हो। Numbers bigger than four चाहिए, तो five और six उठाते हो। बस इतना ही।
तो event even का मतलब set two, four, six, और event bigger than four का मतलब set five, six। दोनों S के subsets हैं।
इसे दिमाग में fix कर लो: event equals subset. जैसे ही events को subsets की तरह देखोगे, आगे के saare rules वही set theory बन जाते हैं जो Chapter one में पढ़ी थी।
Event कब occur करता है? आसान। Event तब occur करता है जब actual outcome उन्हीं cards में से एक हो जो आपने उठाए थे।
Four आया, even event occur हुआ, क्योंकि four set two, four, six के अंदर है। Three आया, नहीं हुआ, क्योंकि three उस set में नहीं है।
Picture में S पूरा box है और A अंदर का circle जिसमें two, four और six हैं। One, three और five S में तो हैं पर A के बाहर, ये outcomes आपके event ने उठाए ही नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: The impossible and the sure event

board_events.text: Two events at the extremes
Scoop up NOTHING → the empty set $\varnothing$ → the IMPOSSIBLE event.
Example: "the die shows a 7." No outcome can ever make it occur.
Scoop up EVERYTHING → the whole of $S$ → the SURE (certain) event.
Example: "the die shows a number from 1 to 6." Some outcome must always make it occur.
"Outcome" ≠ "event": an outcome is one point of S; an event is a set of points.

segments.text: <curious>Two special selections sit right at the edges of what an event can be.</curious> They're the two extremes worth naming carefully.
Scoop up nothing at all. That's the empty set, phi. No outcome can ever land inside an empty selection, so this event can never happen, the impossible event.
The classic example on a die is the event the die shows a seven. There's no seven face on the die, so it simply never occurs.
Now the opposite. Scoop up everything, the whole of S. Whatever outcome shows up is guaranteed to be inside, so this event always happens, the sure or certain event.
On a die, the die shows a number from one to six is the sure event, because every single roll satisfies it.
So hold the two anchors: the impossible event is phi, and the sure event is the whole sample space S.
And one distinction students blur constantly: an outcome is a single point of S, while an event is a set of points, maybe one, maybe many, maybe none. Never treat them as the same word.
दो special selections event की दोनों edges पर बैठी हैं। ये दो extremes हैं जिन्हें ध्यान से नाम देना ज़रूरी है।
कुछ भी मत उठाओ। वो है empty set, phi। किसी outcome के लिए empty selection के अंदर आना possible ही नहीं, तो यह event कभी हो ही नहीं सकता, impossible event।
Die पर classic example है event the die shows a seven। Die पर seven face है ही नहीं, तो यह कभी occur नहीं करता।
अब उल्टा। सब कुछ उठा लो, पूरा S। जो भी outcome आए वो अंदर ही होगा, तो यह event हमेशा होता है, sure या certain event।
Die पर, the die shows a number from one to six sure event है, क्योंकि हर एक roll इसे satisfy करता है।
तो दो anchors पकड़ लो: impossible event है phi, और sure event है पूरा sample space S।
<curious>और एक distinction जो students हमेशा गड़बड़ करते हैं:</curious> outcome S का single point है, जबकि event points का एक set, कभी एक, कभी कई, कभी zero। इन दोनों को एक ही word मत समझो।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: The two silent assumptions behind every event

board_events.text: Two silent assumptions behind every event
Assumption 1: $S$ must be well-defined and COMPLETE — every outcome listed exactly once, none missing.
Mis-specify S and EVERY event built on it is wrong — the #1 silent error in the chapter.
e.g. writing a die's S as {1,2,3,4,5} — one face missing — quietly breaks every event defined next.
Assumption 2: for ordered stages, outcomes are ORDERED pairs.
Toss a coin, then roll a die: $(H,4)$ is a genuine outcome; the order of the stages is baked in.
Collapsing order destroys outcomes and silently shrinks S.

segments.text: Before we count anything, two quiet assumptions hold this whole framework up. Drag them into the light now and you'll dodge most of the chapter's silent errors.
First, the sample space must be well-defined and complete. Every outcome listed exactly once, none missing, none duplicated.
This matters more than it looks. The moment you mis-specify S, every single event built on top of it is wrong. It is the number one silent mistake in this chapter.

A tiny concrete example. Write a die's sample space as one, two, three, four, five, dropping the six, and it looks harmless. But every event you define after that inherits the missing face, so the whole question tilts without a single visible error.
Second, when an experiment happens in ordered stages, the outcomes are ordered pairs, not loose collections.
Toss a coin and then roll a die. The outcome Heads then four is written as the ordered pair H comma four, and the order of the stages is part of the outcome's identity.
If you collapse that order, treating Heads four and four Heads as the same, you quietly destroy outcomes and shrink S without noticing. Keep the order, and keep the sample space honest.
कुछ भी count करने से पहले, दो quiet assumptions इस पूरे framework को खड़ा रखती हैं। इन्हें अभी सामने ले आओ तो chapter की ज़्यादातर silent errors से बच जाओगे।
पहली, sample space well-defined और complete होना चाहिए। हर outcome exactly एक बार listed, ना कोई missing, ना कोई duplicate।
यह दिखने से ज़्यादा important है। जैसे ही आप S को mis-specify करते हो, उस पर बना हर event गलत हो जाता है। यह इस chapter की number one silent mistake है।

एक छोटा concrete example। Die का sample space one, two, three, four, five लिख दो, six छोड़ के, तो harmless लगता है। पर उसके बाद जो भी event define करोगे उसमें missing face inherit हो जाता है, तो पूरा question बिना किसी visible error के गड़बड़ा जाता है।
दूसरी, जब experiment ordered stages में होता है, तो outcomes ordered pairs होते हैं, loose collections नहीं।
Coin toss करो, फिर die roll करो। Outcome Heads फिर four को ordered pair H comma four लिखते हैं, और stages का order outcome की identity का हिस्सा है।
अगर आप वो order collapse कर दो, Heads four और four Heads को same मान लो, तो चुपके से outcomes destroy हो जाते हैं और S छोटा हो जाता है, पता भी नहीं चलता। Order रखो, sample space honest रखो।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: Vocabulary: simple, compound, and counting events

board_events.text: The vocabulary, and counting events
Sample point $\omega$: one element of S. $n(S)$: how many points S has.
SIMPLE (elementary) event: exactly ONE sample point. COMPOUND event: more than one.
An n-outcome sample space has exactly n simple events.
Why $-n-1$? Remove the $n$ singletons and the one empty set.

segments.text: Let's lock down the working vocabulary, then do something the definitions quietly let us do, count the events.
A single element of S is a sample point, written omega. And n of S just means how many sample points S holds, a plain dimensionless count.
Events come in two sizes. A simple, or elementary, event holds exactly one sample point. A compound event holds more than one.
So a sample space with n outcomes has exactly n simple events, one singleton per outcome. Clean, and worth remembering.
Now the surprise. An event is any subset of S, and a set of n elements has two to the power n subsets, so the experiment has two to the power n events in total, counting phi and S themselves.
How many of those are compound? Take the total, two to the power n, and strip out everything that isn't compound.
You remove the n simple events and the one empty event, which leaves two to the power n, minus n, minus one compound events. That subtraction is the whole trick.
पहले working vocabulary पक्की कर लें, फिर वो करें जो definitions चुपके से allow करती हैं, events को count करना।
S का एक single element sample point है, जिसे omega लिखते हैं। और n of S का मतलब बस इतना कि S में कितने sample points हैं, एक plain dimensionless count।
Events दो sizes में आते हैं। Simple, या elementary, event में exactly एक sample point होता है। Compound event में एक से ज़्यादा।
तो n outcomes वाले sample space में exactly n simple events होते हैं, हर outcome का एक singleton। Clean है और याद रखने लायक।
अब surprise। Event S का कोई भी subset है, और n elements वाले set के two to the power n subsets होते हैं, तो experiment के total two to the power n events होते हैं, phi और S समेत।
इनमें से compound कितने? Total लो, two to the power n, और जो compound नहीं है वो सब हटा दो।
आप n simple events और one empty event हटाते हो, जिससे बचते हैं two to the power n, minus n, minus one compound events। यही subtraction पूरा trick है।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: The algebra of events

board_events.text: The algebra of events (set operations)

board_events.latex: A' = S - A = \{\, \omega : \omega \in S \text{ and } \omega \notin A \,\}

board_events.text: Complement $A'$ = the event "NOT A."

board_events.latex: A \cup B \;=\; \text{``A or B''} \;=\; \text{at least one occurs}
A \cap B \;=\; \text{``A and B''} \;=\; \text{both occur together}
A - B \;=\; A \cap B' \;=\; \text{``A but not B''}

board_events.text: "or" → union, "and" → intersection. Translate the English word first.

segments.text: Because events are subsets, combining them is exactly the set algebra from Chapter one, just wearing probability language. Four operations carry the chapter.
The complement of A, written A prime, is S minus A, every outcome that is in the sample space but not in A.
In words, A prime is simply the event not A. If A is the event even, then A prime is the event odd.
A union B means A or B, the event that at least one of the two occurs. Union is generous, it fires if either one shows up.
A intersection B means A and B, the event that both occur together at the same time. Intersection is strict, it needs both.
A minus B, which equals A intersection B prime, is A but not B, the part of A that stays clear of B.

<whisper>Here's the exam habit that saves you:</whisper> translate the English word first. The word or always means union, the word and always means intersection. Get the word right and the set follows.
<curious>क्योंकि events subsets हैं, इन्हें combine करना बिल्कुल वही set algebra है जो Chapter one में थी, बस probability की language में।</curious> चार operations पूरा chapter चलाते हैं।
A का complement, जिसे A prime लिखते हैं, S minus A है, हर वो outcome जो sample space में है पर A में नहीं।
Words में, A prime बस event not A है। अगर A event even है, तो A prime event odd है।
A union B का मतलब A or B, वो event कि दोनों में से at least one occur करे। Union generous है, कोई एक भी आ जाए तो fire करता है।
A intersection B का मतलब A and B, वो event कि दोनों साथ में, एक ही समय पर occur करें। Intersection strict है, दोनों चाहिए।
A minus B, जो equals A intersection B prime, का मतलब A but not B, A का वो हिस्सा जो B से दूर रहता है।
यह exam habit आपको बचाती है: पहले English word translate करो। Word or हमेशा union है, word and हमेशा intersection। Word सही तो set अपने आप सही।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: Mutually exclusive, exhaustive, and partitions

board_events.text: How two events relate
The two events cannot occur together.
At least one of them must occur.

board_events.latex: \text{Partition:}\quad E_i \cap E_j = \varnothing\ (i \ne j)\ \text{ and }\ \bigcup_{i=1}^{n} E_i = S

board_events.text: A partition needs BOTH conditions. Neither alone is enough.

board_events.caption: Not mutually exclusive (left) vs mutually exclusive (right)

segments.text: Examiners love asking how two events sit relative to each other. Three relationships cover almost every question they can throw at you.
Mutually exclusive, also called disjoint, means A intersection B is the empty set.
In plain words, the two events cannot occur together, no single outcome belongs to both. On one roll, getting an even number and getting a three cannot both happen.
Exhaustive means the union of the events fills the entire sample space S.
In plain words, at least one of them must occur, between them they leave no outcome uncovered.
Put both together and you get a partition, the events are pairwise disjoint and their union is all of S. Exactly one occurs, always.

<curious>Careful here, a partition needs both conditions at once.</curious> A set of events can be mutually exclusive without being exhaustive, or exhaustive without being mutually exclusive. Neither property alone makes a partition.

The picture makes it concrete. On the left the circles overlap, so A intersection B is not empty, not mutually exclusive. On the right they sit apart, intersection empty, mutually exclusive. And a fifth idea hides in the word fair: equally likely events are ones where each outcome is as probable as any other.
<curious>Examiners को यह पूछना बहुत पसंद है कि दो events एक-दूसरे के relative कैसे बैठते हैं।</curious> तीन relationships लगभग हर question cover कर लेते हैं।
Mutually exclusive, जिसे disjoint भी कहते हैं, का मतलब A intersection B empty set है।
सीधे शब्दों में, दोनों events साथ occur नहीं कर सकते, कोई single outcome दोनों में नहीं होता। एक ही roll पर even number आना और three आना दोनों साथ possible नहीं।
Exhaustive का मतलब events का union पूरा sample space S भर देता है।
सीधे शब्दों में, इनमें से at least one ज़रूर occur करेगा, मिलकर ये कोई outcome uncovered नहीं छोड़ते।
दोनों को साथ रख दो तो बनता है partition, events pairwise disjoint हैं और इनका union पूरा S है। हमेशा exactly one occur करता है।

यहाँ सावधान, partition के लिए दोनों conditions एक साथ चाहिए। Events का set mutually exclusive हो सकता है बिना exhaustive हुए, या exhaustive बिना mutually exclusive हुए। अकेली कोई एक property partition नहीं बनाती।

Picture इसे concrete कर देती है। बाईं तरफ़ circles overlap कर रहे हैं, तो A intersection B empty नहीं, not mutually exclusive। दाईं तरफ़ वो अलग बैठे हैं, intersection empty, mutually exclusive। और एक पाँचवाँ idea word fair में छिपा है: equally likely events वो हैं जहाँ हर outcome बाक़ी जितना ही probable हो।

board_events.text: Procedure: building the sample space
Step 1: identify what is recorded each trial — "colour AND number," or just "number"? S changes with what you observe.
Step 2 (single stage): list every distinct outcome once.
Step 3 (multi-stage): build a TREE — branch per stage, read each root-to-leaf path as one ordered outcome.
Step 4: with vs. without replacement — "without" removes repeats and shrinks S.

board_events.text: If your hand-built list disagrees with the product, you missed or duplicated a branch.

segments.text: Constructing the sample space is where marks are quietly won or lost. Here is a reliable four-step procedure.
Step one, pin down exactly what you're recording each trial. Are you noting colour and number, or just the number? The sample space changes completely with what you choose to observe.
Step two, for a single-stage experiment, just list every distinct outcome once. For a die, one through six, done.

Step three, for a multi-stage experiment, build a tree. Branch for stage one, sub-branch for stage two, and read each complete root to leaf path as one ordered outcome. The tree mechanically stops you from missing or double counting.
Step four, watch for with versus without replacement. Without replacement removes the repeat outcomes, you can't draw the same ball twice, so it shrinks S.
Step five is a sanity check. For k independent stages, n of S should equal the product of the per-stage counts, m one times m two, and so on.
<whisper>Free error catcher:</whisper> if your hand-built list disagrees with that product, you've missed a branch or duplicated one. Go find it before you count any events.

The tree here is toss a coin, then roll a die. Two coin branches, each splitting into six die branches, gives twelve leaves, H one through H six and T one through T six. Two times six equals twelve, so n of S is twelve, and the product check passes.
Sample space construct करना वो जगह है जहाँ marks चुपचाप बनते या बिगड़ते हैं। यह रहा एक reliable चार-step procedure।
Step one, यह तय करो कि हर trial में exactly क्या record कर रहे हो। Colour and number note कर रहे हो, या सिर्फ़ number? आप जो observe करते हो उसके साथ sample space पूरा बदल जाता है।
Step two, single-stage experiment के लिए, बस हर distinct outcome एक बार list करो। Die के लिए, one से six, हो गया।

Step three, multi-stage experiment के लिए, एक tree बनाओ। Stage one के लिए branch, stage two के लिए sub-branch, और हर पूरा root से leaf path एक ordered outcome की तरह पढ़ो। Tree mechanically आपको miss या double count करने से रोकता है।
Step four, with versus without replacement का ध्यान रखो। Without replacement repeat outcomes हटा देता है, same ball दो बार नहीं draw कर सकते, तो S छोटा हो जाता है।
Step five एक sanity check है। k independent stages के लिए, n of S per-stage counts के product के बराबर होना चाहिए, m one into m two, और आगे।
Free error catcher: अगर आपकी hand-built list उस product से disagree करे, तो कोई branch miss या duplicate हुई है। कोई भी events count करने से पहले उसे ढूंढो।

<curious>यहाँ tree है toss a coin, then roll a die।</curious> दो coin branches, हर एक छह die branches में बँटती है, तो बारह leaves, H one से H six और T one से T six। Two into six equals twelve, तो n of S है twelve, और product check pass हो गया।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: From words to a subset, and testing relationships

board_events.text: Words → subset, and testing relationships
B1: write the full sample space FIRST. Never skip this.
B2: scan every outcome of S, keep only those meeting the condition. That collection IS the event.
Quantifiers: "at least one" ≠ "exactly one" ≠ "at most one." Three phrases, three subsets.
C — mutually exclusive? Compute $A \cap B$; if $= \varnothing$, yes.
C — exhaustive? Compute $A \cup B \cup \cdots$; if $= S$, yes.
C — partition? Both tests must pass together.

segments.text: Two short procedures finish the toolkit: turning a sentence into a subset, and testing how events relate.
For translating a verbal event, step one is non-negotiable, write the full sample space first. Almost every mistake downstream traces back to skipping this.
Step two, scan every outcome in S and keep only the ones that satisfy the condition. That surviving collection is exactly your event, nothing more, nothing less.
<curious>Now the trap examiners live for:</curious> mind the quantifier words. At least one, exactly one, and at most one produce three different subsets from the very same S. Read them slowly.
For testing relationships, to check mutually exclusive, compute A intersection B. If it comes out the empty set, they're mutually exclusive.
To check exhaustive, compute the union A union B and so on. If it equals the whole sample space S, they're exhaustive.
To check partition, both tests must pass at once, disjoint and covering S. A set can pass one and fail the other, so never check just one and assume the rest.
<curious>दो short procedures toolkit पूरा करती हैं:</curious> sentence को subset में बदलना, और events के relationship को test करना।
Verbal event translate करने के लिए, step one non-negotiable है, पहले full sample space लिखो। आगे की लगभग हर mistake इसी को skip करने से आती है।
Step two, S के हर outcome को scan करो और सिर्फ़ वही रखो जो condition satisfy करें। वो बची हुई collection ही exactly आपका event है, ना कम, ना ज़्यादा।
अब वो trap जिसके लिए examiners जीते हैं: quantifier words का ध्यान रखो। At least one, exactly one, और at most one उसी एक S से तीन अलग subsets बनाते हैं। इन्हें धीरे पढ़ो।
Relationships test करने के लिए, mutually exclusive check करने को A intersection B compute करो। अगर empty set निकले, तो mutually exclusive हैं।
Exhaustive check करने को union A union B वगैरह compute करो। अगर पूरे sample space S के बराबर है, तो exhaustive हैं।
Partition check करने को दोनों tests एक साथ pass होने चाहिए, disjoint और S को cover करते हुए। कोई set एक pass और दूसरा fail कर सकता है, तो सिर्फ़ एक check करके बाक़ी assume मत करो।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: Worked example: spinner sample space (CBSE)

board_events.text: Worked Example — spinner (CBSE, 1–2 marks)
A fair spinner has 8 equal sectors numbered 1–8, spun once. Write S, then A = "multiple of 3" and B = "greater than 5."
Since $A \cap B \ne \varnothing$, A and B are NOT mutually exclusive.

segments.text: Let's run a board-level example end to end, a fair spinner, the kind C B S E asks for one or two marks.
The spinner has eight equal sectors numbered one to eight, spun once. We're asked to write the sample space, then express A, multiples of three, and B, numbers greater than five.
Start where you always start, the sample space. Every sector is one outcome recorded once, so S is one through eight and n of S is eight.
Now scan S for multiples of three. Three qualifies, six qualifies, and nothing else up to eight does, so A is the set three, six.
Scan again for numbers greater than five. That's six, seven and eight, so B is the set six, seven, eight.
For the relationship, find what's common to both. Only six sits in A and in B, so A intersection B is the set six.

Since that intersection is not empty, A and B are not mutually exclusive. And notice the presentation order that earns the marks, sample space first, then each event as an explicit set, then the intersection. Same order, every time.
एक board-level example पूरा चलाते हैं, एक fair spinner, जैसा C B S E एक या दो marks के लिए पूछता है।
Spinner में आठ equal sectors हैं, one to eight numbered, एक बार spin करते हैं। पूछा है sample space लिखो, फिर A यानी multiples of three, और B यानी numbers greater than five express करो।
वहीं से शुरू करो जहाँ हमेशा, sample space। हर sector एक outcome है, एक बार record, तो S है one से eight और n of S है eight।
अब S में multiples of three scan करो। Three qualify करता है, six qualify करता है, और eight तक और कुछ नहीं, तो A है set three, six।
फिर से scan करो numbers greater than five के लिए। वो हैं six, seven और eight, तो B है set six, seven, eight।
Relationship के लिए, दोनों में common क्या है ढूंढो। सिर्फ़ six A और B दोनों में है, तो A intersection B है set six।

क्योंकि वो intersection empty नहीं है, A और B mutually exclusive नहीं हैं। और वो presentation order देखो जो marks दिलाता है, पहले sample space, फिर हर event explicit set की तरह, फिर intersection। वही order, हर बार।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: Worked example: which pair is mutually exclusive (CUET)

board_events.text: Speed Trap — which pair is mutually exclusive? (CUET)
One card from a 52-card deck. Which pair is mutually exclusive?
(i) King & Heart  (ii) Spade & red  (iii) face card & Queen  (iv) even-numbered & black
Method: hunt for ONE common card. Find one → not exclusive. Don't enumerate.
(i) King of Hearts is both → overlap → NOT exclusive.
(ii) Spades are black, never red → no overlap → mutually exclusive.
(iii) every Queen is a face card → overlap. (iv) 2 of Spades is even and black → overlap.

segments.text: <excited>This one's a C U E T speed trap.</excited> A multiple choice about which pair of card events is mutually exclusive. The skill being tested is speed, not enumeration.
One card is drawn from a standard fifty two card deck, and we pick which of four pairs of events can never occur together.
The four options are: King and Heart; Spade and red; face card and Queen; and even numbered and black.
Here's the whole method, don't compute full sets. To kill an option, just hunt for a single card sitting in both events. Find one, and they're not mutually exclusive.
Option one, the King of Hearts is both a King and a Heart. One shared card is enough, not mutually exclusive.
Option two, spades are always black, never red. Search as hard as you like, no card is both a spade and red, the overlap is empty, so this pair is mutually exclusive.
Quickly finish the rest to be sure. Every Queen is a face card, so option three overlaps. The two of spades is even and black, so option four overlaps too.
So the answer is option two. The takeaway is the tactic, one counterexample kills an option in a second, never enumerate the whole set under time pressure.
यह एक C U E T speed trap है। Multiple choice कि card events का कौन सा pair mutually exclusive है। यहाँ skill speed की test हो रही है, enumeration की नहीं।
Standard बावन card deck से एक card draw होता है, और हम चुनते हैं कि चार pairs में से कौन सा कभी साथ occur नहीं कर सकता।
चार options हैं: King and Heart; Spade and red; face card and Queen; और even numbered and black।
पूरा method यही है, full sets मत compute करो। किसी option को खत्म करने के लिए, बस एक single card ढूंढो जो दोनों events में हो। एक मिल गया, तो वो mutually exclusive नहीं।
Option one, King of Hearts एक King भी है और Heart भी। एक shared card ही काफ़ी, not mutually exclusive।
Option two, spades हमेशा black होते हैं, कभी red नहीं। जितना मर्ज़ी ढूंढो, कोई card spade और red दोनों नहीं, overlap empty है, तो यह pair mutually exclusive है।
बाक़ी जल्दी से finish करो सुनिश्चित होने को। हर Queen एक face card है, तो option three overlap करता है। Two of spades even और black है, तो option four भी overlap करता है।
<excited>तो answer है option two!</excited> सीख है tactic, एक counterexample किसी option को एक second में खत्म कर देता है, time pressure में पूरा set कभी enumerate मत करो।

segments.text: This J E E Main favourite fuses two skills at once, sample space counting and the partition test. Two distinguishable dice, one red, one blue.
We roll both and record the ordered pair, red then blue. Let A be the event the sum is seven, and C the event the sum is at least eleven.
First n of S. Two independent stages of six outcomes each, and order matters, so n of S is six times six, which is thirty six.
Now list A, the pairs summing to seven, one six, two five, three four, four three, five two, six one. That's six ordered pairs, so n of A is six.
For C, the sum being at least eleven, only three pairs clear the bar of eleven or twelve, five six, six five, and six six.
Are A and C mutually exclusive? Every pair in A sums to seven, and the smallest sum in C is eleven. They cannot share an outcome, so A intersection C is empty, yes, mutually exclusive.

Last part, is A together with A prime a partition? For any event, A intersection A prime is empty and A union A prime is all of S. Both hold, so an event and its complement are always a partition, worth memorising.

यह J E E Main का favourite एक साथ दो skills जोड़ता है, sample space counting और partition test। दो distinguishable dice, एक red, एक blue।
दोनों roll करते हैं और ordered pair record करते हैं, पहले red फिर blue। मान लो A है event the sum is seven, और C है event the sum is at least eleven।
पहले n of S। छह-छह outcomes की दो independent stages, और order matters, तो n of S है six into six, यानी thirty six।
अब A list करो, वो pairs जिनका sum seven है, one six, two five, three four, four three, five two, six one। यह छह ordered pairs हैं, तो n of A है six।
C के लिए, sum at least eleven, सिर्फ़ तीन pairs eleven या twelve का bar पार करते हैं, five six, six five, और six six।
क्या A और C mutually exclusive हैं? A का हर pair seven पर sum करता है, और C में सबसे छोटा sum eleven है। ये कोई outcome share नहीं कर सकते, तो A intersection C empty है, हाँ, mutually exclusive।

आख़िरी part, क्या A और A prime मिलकर partition हैं? किसी भी event के लिए, A intersection A prime empty है और A union A prime पूरा S है। दोनों hold करते हैं, तो event और उसका complement हमेशा एक partition है, याद रखने लायक।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: Worked example: counting events abstractly (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: Counting events abstractly (JEE Advanced)
A sample space has exactly n distinct outcomes ($n \ge 2$). (a) How many events (subsets, incl. $\varnothing$ and S)?
Key fact: an n-element set has $2^n$ subsets.
(b) How many are compound?
(c) Unordered pairs $\{A,B\}$ of non-empty mutually exclusive events:

segments.text: Now the J E E Advanced flavour, pure counting of events, no dice, just structure. The sample space has exactly n distinct outcomes, with n at least two.
Part a asks how many distinct events the experiment has, counting both the empty set and S itself.
Here's the key fact: an event is any subset of an n element set, and a set of size n has two to the power n subsets.
So the number of events is simply two to the power n. That single fact drives the whole problem.
Part b, how many of those are compound, meaning more than one point?
Take the total, two to the power n, remove the n singleton events and the one empty event, and you get two to the power n, minus n, minus one.

Part c is the hard one, count unordered pairs of non empty events that are mutually exclusive. Assign each of the n outcomes to one of three bins, only A, only B, or neither, giving three to the power n assignments.

<whisper>Now clean up carefully.</whisper> Subtract the cases making A empty, two to the power n, and those making B empty, another two to the power n, then add back the one counted twice. That gives three to the power n minus two times two to the power n plus one for ordered pairs. Halve it, since the pair is unordered, to get this final formula. Check it at n equals two, it gives one, and indeed there's exactly one such pair.
अब J E E Advanced का flavour, events की pure counting, कोई dice नहीं, बस structure। Sample space में exactly n distinct outcomes हैं, n कम से कम two।
Part a पूछता है experiment के कितने distinct events हैं, empty set और S दोनों को गिनते हुए।
<curious>Key fact यह है:</curious> event n element set का कोई भी subset है, और size n के set के two to the power n subsets होते हैं।
तो number of events बस two to the power n है। यही एक fact पूरे problem को चलाता है।
Part b, इनमें से compound कितने, यानी एक से ज़्यादा point वाले?
Total लो, two to the power n, n singleton events और one empty event हटाओ, और मिलता है two to the power n, minus n, minus one।

Part c मुश्किल है, non empty events के unordered pairs गिनो जो mutually exclusive हों। हर n outcome को तीन bins में से एक में डालो, only A, only B, या neither, जिससे मिलते हैं three to the power n assignments।

अब सावधानी से clean up करो। A को empty बनाने वाले cases घटाओ, two to the power n, और B को empty बनाने वाले, एक और two to the power n, फिर जो दो बार गिना गया उसे add back करो। इससे ordered pairs के लिए मिलता है three to the power n minus two into two to the power n plus one। इसे half करो, क्योंकि pair unordered है, तो यह final formula बनती है। n equals two पर check करो, यह one देता है, और सच में exactly एक ऐसा pair है।

sections.subtopic: Sample Space and Events
sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Pitfalls & Pro-Tips
1. Outcome ≠ event. "Write the event" wants a SET — write {4}, not 4.
2. Mutually exclusive ⇏ exhaustive. Test $A \cap B$ and $A \cup B$ separately.
3. A mis-built S from a multi-stage experiment poisons every later event — draw the tree.
4. Early warning: mutually exclusive is NOT the same as independent (a Class 12 trap).

board_events.latex: \text{mutually exclusive} \;\Leftrightarrow\; A \cap B = \varnothing \quad (\text{about SETS, not probabilities})

board_events.text: Pro-Tip: to check mutually exclusive, hunt for ONE common outcome — a search, not a calculation.

segments.text: Let's close the subtopic with the mistakes that quietly cost marks, and the one habit that saves time.

Pitfall one, confusing an outcome with an event. Getting a four is an outcome; getting an even number is an event, the set two, four, six. When a question says write the event, it wants a set, write brace four brace, not a bare four, even for a single point.

<whisper>Pitfall two, assuming mutually exclusive implies exhaustive, or the reverse.</whisper> They're independent conditions. On a die, the event one and the event two are mutually exclusive but nowhere near exhaustive. Always test the intersection and the union separately.

Pitfall three, a mis-built sample space from a multi stage experiment. Forget without replacement, or collapse the ordered pairs, and you silently poison every event after it. The tree costs ten seconds and saves the whole question.
Pitfall four is an early warning for Class twelve, students start treating mutually exclusive and independent as the same thing. They are nearly opposites.

Plant the flag now, mutually exclusive means A intersection B is empty. That's a statement about the sets, not about probabilities. Independence, which multiplies probabilities, is a completely different idea you'll meet next year.

And the pro tip that speeds up every mutually exclusive question, you never need the full intersection. Just hunt for one outcome sitting in both events. Find one and stop, not exclusive. Scan and find none, mutually exclusive. You've turned a calculation into a one second search.
Subtopic को उन mistakes के साथ close करते हैं जो चुपचाप marks खा जाती हैं, और वो एक habit जो time बचाती है।

Pitfall one, outcome को event समझ लेना। Four आना एक outcome है; even number आना एक event है, set two, four, six। जब question कहे write the event, तो उसे set चाहिए, brace four brace लिखो, अकेला four नहीं, single point के लिए भी।

Pitfall two, यह मान लेना कि mutually exclusive का मतलब exhaustive है, या उल्टा। ये independent conditions हैं। Die पर, event one और event two mutually exclusive हैं पर exhaustive के आसपास भी नहीं। हमेशा intersection और union अलग-अलग test करो।

Pitfall three, multi stage experiment से mis-built sample space। Without replacement भूल जाओ, या ordered pairs collapse कर दो, तो उसके बाद का हर event चुपके से poison हो जाता है। Tree दस second लेता है और पूरा question बचा लेता है।
Pitfall four Class twelve के लिए early warning है, students mutually exclusive और independent को same चीज़ मानने लगते हैं। ये लगभग opposites हैं।

अभी झंडा गाड़ दो, mutually exclusive का मतलब A intersection B empty है। यह sets के बारे में statement है, probabilities के बारे में नहीं। Independence, जो probabilities को multiply करती है, बिल्कुल अलग idea है जो अगले साल मिलेगा।

<whisper>और वो pro tip जो हर mutually exclusive question तेज़ कर देती है:</whisper> आपको कभी full intersection नहीं चाहिए। बस एक outcome ढूंढो जो दोनों events में हो। एक मिला और रुक जाओ, not exclusive। Scan किया और कोई नहीं मिला, mutually exclusive। आपने calculation को एक second की search बना दिया।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: How likely? The classical definition

board_events.text: How LIKELY is an event?
Assigning a number — a probability — to each event is the whole job of this subtopic.
Roll a fair die: the chance of an even number is 3 good faces out of 6.
Favourable outcomes over total outcomes — the CLASSICAL definition.
Intuitive and, for fair dice and well-shuffled cards, completely correct.

segments.text: The first subtopic taught us to lay out every outcome and scoop the ones we care about into an event. But we never answered the obvious next question. How likely is that event?
<curious>Assigning a number, a probability, to each event is the entire job of this subtopic.</curious> And you've met probability informally before, so let's start from what you already trust.
Roll a fair die and ask for the chance of an even number. Three faces are good, two, four and six, out of six faces in total.
So the probability of even is three over six, which is one half. Nothing mysterious yet.
That recipe, favourable outcomes over total outcomes, is the classical definition of probability. It's the one you grew up with.
In symbols, P of E equals n of E over n of S, favourable count on top, total count below.
And for fair dice and well shuffled cards it is wonderfully intuitive and completely correct. The trouble starts only when the world stops being fair, which is the next section.
<curious>पहले subtopic ने सिखाया हर outcome को lay out करना और जो चाहिए उन्हें event में scoop करना।</curious> पर हमने अगला obvious सवाल कभी answer नहीं किया। वो event कितना likely है?
हर event को एक number, यानी probability, assign करना ही इस पूरे subtopic का काम है। और probability आप पहले informally मिल चुके हो, तो जो पहले से trust करते हो वहीं से शुरू करें।
एक fair die roll करो और even number का chance पूछो। तीन faces good हैं, two, four और six, कुल छह faces में से।
तो probability of even है three over six, यानी one half। अभी तक कुछ mysterious नहीं।
वो recipe, favourable outcomes over total outcomes, probability की classical definition है। वही जो बचपन से आती है।
Symbols में, P of E equals n of E over n of S, favourable count ऊपर, total count नीचे।
और fair dice और well shuffled cards के लिए यह wonderfully intuitive और completely correct है। दिक्कत तब शुरू होती है जब दुनिया fair रहना बंद कर दे, जो अगला section है।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: Three cracks in the classical recipe

board_events.text: Three cracks in the classical recipe
Crack 1: it only works when every outcome is EQUALLY LIKELY.
A tossed drawing pin: point-up vs point-down are NOT equally likely, so "1 out of 2" is nonsense.
Crack 2: it collapses with infinitely many outcomes.
"Pick a random natural number" — there is no finite total to divide by.
Crack 3: "equally likely" already means "equally probable" — defining probability using probability. Circular.
Mathematicians dislike circles — the classical recipe needs a firmer foundation.

segments.text: The classical recipe is intuitive, but it hides three cracks. Once you see them, you'll understand why we need something sturdier.
Crack one, it only works when every outcome is equally likely. That assumption is doing silent, heavy lifting.
Toss a drawing pin. There are two outcomes, point up and point down, but they are emphatically not equally likely, so one out of two is nonsense here.
Crack two, the recipe collapses the moment there are infinitely many outcomes.
Ask for the probability of picking a random natural number. There is no finite total sitting underneath to divide by, so the formula has nothing to work with.

<curious>Crack three is the deepest, and the N C E R T text points right at it.</curious> The definition quietly uses the words equally likely, which already mean equally probable, so we're defining probability in terms of probability. That's a circular definition.
And mathematicians dislike circles. So however comfortable the classical recipe feels, it needs a firmer foundation underneath it.
Classical recipe intuitive है, पर इसमें तीन cracks छिपी हैं। एक बार दिख जाएं, तो समझ आएगा कि हमें कुछ मज़बूत क्यों चाहिए।
Crack one, यह सिर्फ़ तब काम करता है जब हर outcome equally likely हो। वो assumption चुपचाप बहुत भारी काम कर रही है।
एक drawing pin toss करो। दो outcomes हैं, point up और point down, पर ये बिल्कुल equally likely नहीं, तो यहाँ one out of two बकवास है।
Crack two, जैसे ही infinitely many outcomes हों, recipe collapse कर जाती है।
Random natural number pick करने की probability पूछो। नीचे कोई finite total है ही नहीं जिससे divide करें, तो formula के पास काम करने को कुछ नहीं।

Crack three सबसे गहरी है, और N C E R T text इसी की तरफ़ इशारा करता है। Definition चुपके से words equally likely use करती है, जिनका मतलब पहले से equally probable है, तो हम probability को probability से define कर रहे हैं। यह circular definition है।
<curious>और mathematicians circles को नापसंद करते हैं।</curious> तो classical recipe चाहे कितनी भी comfortable लगे, इसके नीचे एक मज़बूत foundation चाहिए।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: Kolmogorov's fix: the axiomatic approach

board_events.text: Kolmogorov's fix: the axiomatic approach
Don't define what probability IS — list the rules any sensible probability must obey.
Anything obeying those rules is declared a legitimate probability.
Same move as Euclid: never defines "point" or "line" — states axioms, then reasons.
Picture 1 kg of sand spread across the outcomes of an experiment.
Each outcome gets some NON-NEGATIVE sand (possibly zero); the total is exactly 1 kg.
P(event) = how much sand sits on the outcomes inside it.

segments.text: So here is the fix, and it's beautifully sneaky. It came from the Russian mathematician Kolmogorov in nineteen thirty three.
Instead of trying to define what probability is, he simply listed the rules any sensible probability must obey.
Then he declared anything that obeys those rules to be a legitimate probability. That inversion is the whole axiomatic approach.
It's the exact move geometry makes. Euclid never defines point or line from scratch. He states the axioms they must satisfy and reasons from there.
<excited>Here's the picture that makes it click.</excited> Imagine spreading one full kilogram of sand across the outcomes of your experiment.
Each outcome gets some non negative amount of sand, possibly zero, and the total sand across the whole sample space is exactly one kilogram.
The probability of an event is then just how much sand sits on the outcomes inside that event. That's it, weigh the sand.

A fair die spreads the sand evenly, one sixth of a kilogram per face. A loaded die piles more onto some faces than others. Both are perfectly valid, because both obey the same two rules, no negative sand and one kilogram total.
तो यह रहा fix, और यह बहुत sneaky है। यह आया Russian mathematician Kolmogorov से, नाइनटीन थर्टी थ्री में।
Probability क्या है यह define करने की कोशिश करने के बजाय, उसने बस वो rules list कर दिए जो किसी भी sensible probability को माननी हों।
<excited>फिर उसने declare कर दिया कि जो कुछ भी उन rules को obey करे वो legitimate probability है।</excited> यही inversion पूरा axiomatic approach है।
यह बिल्कुल वही move है जो geometry करती है। Euclid point या line को scratch से define नहीं करता। वो बस axioms बताता है जो उन्हें satisfy करनी हैं और वहीं से reason करता है।
यह रही वो picture जिससे बात clear हो जाती है। सोचो एक पूरा किलोग्राम sand को अपने experiment के outcomes पर फैला रहे हो।
हर outcome को कुछ non negative sand मिलती है, possibly zero, और पूरे sample space पर total sand exactly one kilogram है।
किसी event की probability बस इतनी है कि उस event के अंदर के outcomes पर कितनी sand बैठी है। बस, sand तौल लो।

एक fair die sand को evenly फैलाता है, हर face पर one sixth kilogram। एक loaded die कुछ faces पर ज़्यादा ढेर लगाता है। दोनों बिल्कुल valid हैं, क्योंकि दोनों वही दो rules obey करते हैं, कोई negative sand नहीं और total one kilogram।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: What the axioms quietly assume

board_events.text: What the axioms quietly assume
The Class 11 axioms are stated for FINITE sample spaces.
Kolmogorov's full theory covers infinite S too, but the Class 11 form stays finite.
Additivity is only guaranteed for MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE events — when they don't overlap.
$P(E) = \dfrac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ is NOT an axiom — it appears only when all outcomes are equally likely.
Apply $n(E)/n(S)$ to a loaded die and you get a wrong answer that looks right.
When outcomes aren't equally likely, go back to the axioms and sum the actual sand.

segments.text: Before we list the rules formally, know what they quietly assume, so you don't misapply them later.
First, the axioms in the form you need for Class eleven are stated for finite sample spaces, a listable, countable set of outcomes.
Kolmogorov's full theory reaches infinite sample spaces as well, but the version you need in Class eleven deliberately stays finite, which keeps the algebra clean.
Second, additivity, the rule that lets you add probabilities, is only guaranteed for mutually exclusive events. When events overlap, plain addition breaks.

<whisper>And here's the one that trips everyone:</whisper> the familiar formula P of E equals n of E over n of S is not an axiom. It's a special case that appears only when all outcomes are equally likely.
Forget that caveat and apply n of E over n of S to a loaded die, and you'll get a confident, wrong answer that looks perfectly right on the page.
So the rule is simple, when outcomes are not equally likely, don't reach for the counting formula. Go back to the axioms and sum the actual sand on each outcome.
Rules को formally list करने से पहले, जान लो कि ये चुपके से क्या assume करती हैं, ताकि बाद में इन्हें गलत जगह न लगाओ।
पहला, Class eleven के लिए जिस form में axioms चाहिए वो finite sample spaces के लिए बताई गई हैं, एक listable, countable set of outcomes।
Kolmogorov की पूरी theory infinite sample spaces तक भी पहुँचती है, पर Class eleven में जो version चाहिए वो जानबूझकर finite रहता है, जिससे algebra साफ़ रहती है।
दूसरा, additivity, वो rule जो probabilities जोड़ने देता है, सिर्फ़ mutually exclusive events के लिए guaranteed है। जब events overlap करें, plain addition टूट जाता है।
और यह रही वो जो सबको गिराती है: familiar formula P of E equals n of E over n of S कोई axiom नहीं है। यह एक special case है जो सिर्फ़ तब निकलता है जब saare outcomes equally likely हों।
<whisper>वो caveat भूल जाओ और n of E over n of S एक loaded die पर लगा दो, तो एक confident, गलत answer मिलेगा जो page पर बिल्कुल सही लगता है।</whisper>
तो rule आसान है, जब outcomes equally likely न हों, counting formula की तरफ़ मत जाओ। Axioms पर वापस जाओ और हर outcome पर actual sand जोड़ो।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: The three axioms and probability via sample points

board_events.text: The three axioms of probability (Kolmogorov)

board_events.latex: \text{Axiom 3 (Additivity):}\quad A \cap B = \varnothing \;\Rightarrow\; P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)

board_events.text: Probability via sample points: assign each $\omega_i$ a number $P(\omega_i)$.
All probabilities are dimensionless numbers in $[0,1]$ — the only "unit check" is: does it lie in [0, 1]?

segments.text: Here is the entire foundation, three short axioms. Everything else in the chapter is squeezed out of these.
Axiom one, non negativity: the probability of any event A is greater than or equal to zero. No negative sand, ever.
Axiom two, normalization: the probability of the whole sample space S is exactly one. All the sand, one kilogram, always accounted for.
Axiom three, additivity: if A and B are mutually exclusive, so A intersection B is empty, then the probability of A union B is simply P of A plus P of B. Non overlapping sand piles just add.
There's a companion picture at the outcome level. Assign each sample point omega i its own number, P of omega i.
Two conditions bind them: every P of omega i is non negative, and they all sum to one across S. That's the sand rule stated point by point.
Then the probability of any event E is just the sum of the sand on the outcomes inside E. Add up the points, get the event.

<whisper>One more habit worth keeping.</whisper> Every probability is a dimensionless number between zero and one, so your only unit check is asking, does my answer lie between zero and one? If not, it's an error.
<curious>यह रही पूरी foundation, तीन छोटी axioms।</curious> Chapter का बाक़ी सब कुछ इन्हीं से निचोड़ा जाता है।
Axiom one, non negativity: किसी भी event A की probability greater than or equal to zero है। कभी कोई negative sand नहीं।
Axiom two, normalization: पूरे sample space S की probability exactly one है। पूरी sand, one kilogram, हमेशा accounted for।
Axiom three, additivity: अगर A और B mutually exclusive हैं, यानी A intersection B empty है, तो P of A union B बस P of A plus P of B है। अलग-अलग sand piles बस जुड़ जाते हैं।
एक companion picture outcome level पर भी है। हर sample point omega i को उसका अपना number assign करो, P of omega i।
दो conditions इन्हें बाँधती हैं: हर P of omega i non negative है, और ये सब S पर मिलकर one बनते हैं। यही sand rule point by point।
फिर किसी भी event E की probability बस E के अंदर के outcomes की sand का sum है। Points जोड़ो, event मिल गया।
एक habit और रखने लायक। हर probability zero और one के बीच का dimensionless number है, तो आपका इकलौता unit check यही है, क्या मेरा answer zero और one के बीच है? नहीं तो error है।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: The working toolkit of consequences

board_events.text: The working toolkit (all derived next)

board_events.latex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
P(\text{exactly one of } A, B) = P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A \cap B)

segments.text: <curious>Before deriving anything, here's the toolkit you'll actually use in problems.</curious> Every line comes straight out of the three axioms, which we prove in the next sections.
First the anchors: every probability sits between zero and one, the impossible event has probability zero, and the sure event has probability one.
The complement law, the not law: P of A prime equals one minus P of A. This single line is the highest leverage trick in the chapter.
The equally likely special case: P of A equals n of A over n of S, and remember, only when outcomes are equally likely.
The general addition rule: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A intersection B. The subtraction fixes double counting.
When A and B are mutually exclusive, the overlap is zero, so it collapses to just P of A plus P of B.
For exactly one of A and B, you exclude the overlap from both sides: P of A plus P of B minus two times P of A intersection B.
And by De Morgan, the probability of neither, A prime intersection B prime, is one minus P of A union B. Six lines, one foundation.
कुछ भी derive करने से पहले, यह रहा वो toolkit जो problems में सच में use होगा। हर line सीधे तीन axioms से निकलती है, जो अगले sections में prove करेंगे।
पहले anchors: हर probability zero और one के बीच है, impossible event की probability zero, और sure event की probability one।
<excited>Complement law, यानी not law: P of A prime equals one minus P of A.</excited> यह इकलौती line chapter की highest leverage trick है।
Equally likely special case: P of A equals n of A over n of S, और याद रखो, सिर्फ़ तब जब outcomes equally likely हों।
General addition rule: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A intersection B। वो subtraction double counting ठीक करता है।
जब A और B mutually exclusive हों, overlap zero है, तो यह बस P of A plus P of B रह जाता है।
Exactly one of A and B के लिए, overlap को दोनों तरफ़ से हटाते हो: P of A plus P of B minus two into P of A intersection B।
और De Morgan से, neither की probability, A prime intersection B prime, one minus P of A union B है। छह lines, एक foundation।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: Deriving the first three results (impossible, complement, bounds)

board_events.text: R1–R3: squeezing results from the axioms
R1 — $S$ and $\varnothing$ are mutually exclusive, and $S \cup \varnothing = S$. Apply Axiom 3:
R2 — $A$ and $A'$ are mutually exclusive and exhaust $S$. Apply Axiom 3, then Axiom 2:

board_events.latex: P(A) + P(A') = P(A \cup A') = P(S) = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; P(A') = 1 - P(A)

board_events.text: R3 — lower bound is Axiom 1; upper bound comes from R2:

segments.text: <curious>Now watch the toolkit fall out of the axioms.</curious> See this once and you'll never need to memorise the table.
Result one, the impossible event has probability zero. The sure event S and the empty set are mutually exclusive, and their union is just S again.

Apply axiom three: P of S equals P of S union empty, which equals P of S plus P of empty. Cancel P of S from both sides and you're left with P of empty equals zero. An outcome that can never happen carries zero sand.
Result two, the complement law. An event A and its complement A prime are mutually exclusive and together exhaust S, that partition fact from the first subtopic.
Apply axiom three, then axiom two: P of A plus P of A prime equals P of A union A prime, which equals P of S, which equals one. Rearrange and P of A prime equals one minus P of A.
<excited>This complement law is the single most useful line in the chapter.</excited> Whenever at least one is hard, compute none and subtract. Result three then follows almost for free.

The lower bound is axiom one directly, P of A is at least zero. For the upper bound, write P of A as one minus P of A prime, and since P of A prime is at least zero, P of A is at most one. So every probability is trapped in zero to one, no exceptions.
अब देखो toolkit axioms से कैसे गिरता है। एक बार यह देख लो तो table कभी memorise करने की ज़रूरत नहीं।
<curious>Result one, impossible event की probability zero।</curious> Sure event S और empty set mutually exclusive हैं, और इनका union बस फिर से S है।

Axiom three लगाओ: P of S equals P of S union empty, जो equals P of S plus P of empty। दोनों तरफ़ से P of S cancel करो और बचता है P of empty equals zero। जो outcome कभी हो ही नहीं सकता वो zero sand रखता है।
Result two, complement law। एक event A और उसका complement A prime mutually exclusive हैं और मिलकर S को exhaust करते हैं, वही partition fact पहले subtopic से।
Axiom three, फिर axiom two लगाओ: P of A plus P of A prime equals P of A union A prime, जो equals P of S, जो equals one। Rearrange करो और P of A prime equals one minus P of A।
यह complement law chapter की इकलौती सबसे useful line है। जब भी at least one मुश्किल हो, none compute करो और subtract कर दो। Result three फिर लगभग मुफ़्त में आ जाता है।

Lower bound सीधे axiom one है, P of A कम से कम zero। Upper bound के लिए, P of A को one minus P of A prime लिखो, और चूँकि P of A prime कम से कम zero है, P of A ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा one। तो हर probability zero से one में फँसी है, कोई exception नहीं।

sections.title: Deriving the general addition rule

board_events.text: R4 — why we subtract the overlap
Carve $A \cup B$ into two disjoint slabs: all of $A$, plus the part of $B$ outside $A$.

board_events.latex: A \cup B = A \cup (B - A), \qquad A \cap (B - A) = \varnothing

board_events.text: Now carve $B$ into its overlap with $A$ and its non-overlap:

board_events.latex: P(B) = P(A \cap B) + P(B - A) \;\Rightarrow\; P(B - A) = P(B) - P(A \cap B)

board_events.caption: The lens A∩B is counted twice — subtract it once
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 380 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="15" width="360" height="160" rx="6" fill="#fdf6e3" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="24" y="36" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#333">S</text><defs><clipPath id="lensA"><circle cx="150" cy="95" r="70"/></clipPath></defs><circle cx="150" cy="95" r="70" fill="#ffd9a0" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="#c8862a" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="230" cy="95" r="70" fill="#a9d6c4" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="#2a8c6a" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="230" cy="95" r="70" fill="#d98c4a" fill-opacity="0.55" stroke="none" clip-path="url(#lensA)"/><text x="112" y="100" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">A</text><text x="268" y="100" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">B</text><text x="190" y="99" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6a2f0c">A∩B</text><text x="190" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#a33">the lens is counted twice in P(A)+P(B) — subtract once</text><text x="190" y="232" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#333">P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B)</text></svg>

segments.text: The general addition rule is the step students most want to memorise and least understand. So let's build it, not memorise it. The trick is to carve overlapping events into disjoint pieces, because axiom three only works on disjoint pieces.
Carve A union B into two slabs that don't overlap: all of A, plus the part of B that lies outside A.
Those two slabs, A and B minus A, are disjoint by construction, their intersection is empty.
So axiom three applies cleanly: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus A.
Now do the same carving to B itself, split it into its overlap with A and its non overlap.
Axiom three again gives P of B equals P of A intersection B plus P of B minus A. Rearrange for P of B minus A, it's P of B minus P of A intersection B.
Substitute that back, and out drops the rule: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A intersection B.

<curious>And here's the why, in one picture.</curious> P of A plus P of B counts the lens, the intersection, twice, once in each event. So we subtract one copy to fix the double count. If A and B are mutually exclusive, the lens is empty, the subtracted term is zero, and we're back to plain axiom three.

<curious>General addition rule वो step है जिसे students सबसे ज़्यादा memorise करना चाहते हैं और सबसे कम समझते हैं।</curious> तो इसे बनाते हैं, memorise नहीं करते। Trick है overlapping events को disjoint pieces में काटना, क्योंकि axiom three सिर्फ़ disjoint pieces पर काम करता है।
A union B को दो slabs में काटो जो overlap न करें: पूरा A, plus B का वो हिस्सा जो A के बाहर है।
वो दो slabs, A और B minus A, construction से disjoint हैं, इनका intersection empty है।
तो axiom three साफ़-साफ़ लगता है: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus A।
अब यही carving B पर करो, इसे A के साथ overlap और non overlap में बाँटो।
Axiom three फिर देता है P of B equals P of A intersection B plus P of B minus A। P of B minus A के लिए rearrange करो, वो है P of B minus P of A intersection B।
उसे वापस substitute करो, और rule निकल आता है: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A intersection B।

और यह रहा why, एक picture में। P of A plus P of B उस lens को, यानी intersection को, दो बार गिनता है, हर event में एक बार। तो हम एक copy subtract करके double count ठीक करते हैं। अगर A और B mutually exclusive हों, lens empty है, subtracted term zero है, और हम वापस plain axiom three पर।

sections.title: Deriving the equally-likely formula

board_events.text: R5 — the classical recipe, recovered as a theorem
Suppose all $n(S)$ outcomes are equally likely, each carrying the same $p$.
An event $A$ with $n(A)$ points sums that many equal pieces of sand:
Sanity: a single-point event gives $1/n(S)$ — e.g. one face of a fair die.
So $n(A)/n(S)$ is a THEOREM, not a definition — and it holds only under equal likelihood.

segments.text: Finally, let's recover the old classical recipe, but this time as a theorem that falls out of the axioms, not as a definition we assumed.
Suppose all n of S outcomes are equally likely, so each sample point carries the same probability, call it p.
Normalization says the sand totals one, so n of S times p equals one, which means p is one over n of S.
Now take an event A holding n of A points. Its probability is just the sum of that many equal pieces of sand.
That sum is n of A copies of one over n of S, which is n of A over n of S. There's your classical formula, rebuilt from the axioms.
Sanity check it on a single outcome. An event with just one point gives one over n of S, exactly the one sixth you'd expect for one face of a fair die.

<whisper>But notice what we just proved.</whisper> n of A over n of S is a theorem, a consequence, not a definition, and it holds only under the equally likely assumption. That's exactly why it fails on a loaded die.
आख़िर में, पुरानी classical recipe को recover करते हैं, पर इस बार एक theorem की तरह जो axioms से निकलती है, न कि एक definition की तरह जो हमने मान ली थी।
मान लो saare n of S outcomes equally likely हैं, तो हर sample point वही probability रखता है, उसे p कहो।
Normalization कहता है sand का total one है, तो n of S into p equals one, यानी p है one over n of S।
अब एक event A लो जिसमें n of A points हैं। इसकी probability बस उतने equal sand pieces का sum है।
<whisper>वो sum है n of A copies of one over n of S, यानी n of A over n of S।</whisper> यह रही आपकी classical formula, axioms से फिर बनी।
इसे single outcome पर sanity check करो। सिर्फ़ एक point वाला event देता है one over n of S, बिल्कुल वही one sixth जो fair die के एक face के लिए expect करते हो।
पर देखो हमने अभी क्या prove किया। n of A over n of S एक theorem है, एक consequence, definition नहीं, और यह सिर्फ़ equally likely assumption के तहत hold करता है। इसीलिए यह loaded die पर fail होता है।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: Worked example: coloured marbles (CBSE)

board_events.text: Worked Example — marbles (CBSE, 2–3 marks)
Box: 4 red, 5 green, 3 blue. One marble drawn at random. Find P(red), P(not blue), P(red or green).
Sanity check: not-blue = red-or-green (the only non-red-non-green marble is blue). Both give 3/4. ✓

segments.text: A clean C B S E numerical, worth two or three marks, that exercises three different tools in one problem.
The box holds four red, five green and three blue marbles, identical except for colour, and we draw one at random. We want the probability of red, of not blue, and of red or green.
Total marbles: four plus five plus three is twelve, and since they're identical they're equally likely, so the counting formula is fair game here.
Probability of red is n of red over n of S, four over twelve, which reduces to one third.
For not blue, use the complement law. Blue is three over twelve, so not blue is one minus that, which is three quarters. Complement beats listing every non blue marble.
Red or green are mutually exclusive, a marble can't be both, so by additivity just add: four twelfths plus five twelfths is nine twelfths, or three quarters.

<whisper>And a lovely built in check.</whisper> Not blue and red or green describe the same set, because the only way to be neither red nor green is to be blue. Both came out three quarters, so the answer is consistent.
<curious>एक साफ़ C B S E numerical, दो या तीन marks का, जो एक ही problem में तीन अलग tools चलाता है।</curious>
Box में चार red, पाँच green और तीन blue marbles हैं, colour के अलावा identical, और हम एक random draw करते हैं। हमें चाहिए probability of red, of not blue, और of red or green।
Total marbles: चार plus पाँच plus तीन यानी twelve, और चूँकि ये identical हैं ये equally likely हैं, तो counting formula यहाँ fair game है।
Probability of red है n of red over n of S, four over twelve, जो reduce होकर one third।
Not blue के लिए, complement law use करो। Blue है three over twelve, तो not blue है one minus that, यानी three quarters। Complement हर non blue marble list करने से बेहतर है।
Red or green mutually exclusive हैं, एक marble दोनों नहीं हो सकता, तो additivity से बस add करो: four twelfths plus five twelfths यानी nine twelfths, या three quarters।
और एक प्यारा built in check। Not blue और red or green एक ही set बताते हैं, क्योंकि neither red nor green होने का इकलौता तरीका blue होना है। दोनों three quarters निकले, तो answer consistent है।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: Worked example: which probability assignment is valid (CUET)

board_events.text: Speed Trap — which assignment is valid? (CUET)
$S = \{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3, \omega_4\}$. Which is a valid probability assignment?
Test only two axioms: all values ≥ 0 (Axiom 1) AND sum = 1 (normalization).
(ii) contains −0.1 < 0 → dead instantly (scan for a negative first).
(i) sums to 1.2 and (iv) to 1.1 — both ≠ 1, fail normalization.

segments.text: This C U E T one liner tests whether you actually know the axioms, disguised as a which is valid question. Speed comes from checking only what matters.
The sample space has four outcomes, and we're given four candidate probability assignments, one per option.
The four rows of numbers are the candidates, your job is to find the single legal one.
You only ever test two things, are all values non negative, that's axiom one, and do they sum to one, that's normalization. Nothing fancier.
Scan for a negative first, it kills an option in one glance. Option two has minus zero point one, so it's dead instantly, no addition needed.
Now add the rest. Option one sums to one point two and option four to one point one, so both fail normalization, they don't total one.

<excited>Only option three survives.</excited> Its values are all non negative and sum to exactly one point zero, so option three is valid. The tactic: hunt a negative, then check the sum, never anything more.
<excited>यह C U E T one liner test करता है कि आप axioms सच में जानते हो या नहीं, which is valid question के भेस में।</excited> Speed सिर्फ़ ज़रूरी चीज़ check करने से आती है।
Sample space में चार outcomes हैं, और हमें चार candidate probability assignments दिए हैं, हर option के लिए एक।
Numbers की चार rows ही candidates हैं, आपका काम इकलौती legal वाली ढूंढना है।
आप बस दो चीज़ें test करते हो, क्या saare values non negative हैं, वो axiom one, और क्या ये मिलकर one बनते हैं, वो normalization। इससे fancy कुछ नहीं।
पहले negative scan करो, एक नज़र में option खत्म। Option two में minus zero point one है, तो तुरंत dead, कोई addition नहीं चाहिए।
अब बाक़ी add करो। Option one one point two बनता है और option four one point one, तो दोनों normalization fail, ये one नहीं बनते।
सिर्फ़ option three बचता है। इसके values saare non negative हैं और मिलकर exactly one point zero बनते हैं, तो option three valid है। Tactic: negative ढूंढो, फिर sum check करो, इससे ज़्यादा कभी नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: Worked example: addition-rule composition (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Two events, three questions (JEE Main)
$P(A)=0.6,\ P(B)=0.5,\ P(A\cap B)=0.3$. Find P(A∪B), P(exactly one), P(A'∩B').
Cross-check: $P(A \cup B) - P(A \cap B) = 0.8 - 0.3 = 0.5$ ✓
Pattern: the addition rule feeds the complement-of-a-union — the JEE Main signature.

segments.text: A staple J E E Main composition, one setup feeding three linked questions. Two events with known probabilities and a known overlap.
We're told P of A is zero point six, P of B is zero point five, and P of A intersection B is zero point three. Find the union, exactly one, and neither.
Part a, the general addition rule: zero point six plus zero point five minus zero point three is zero point eight. That's P of A union B.

Part b, exactly one strips the overlap from both sides, so P of A plus P of B minus twice P of A intersection B, that's zero point six plus zero point five minus zero point six, which is zero point five.
Nice cross check, exactly one also equals P of A union B minus P of A intersection B, zero point eight minus zero point three, again zero point five. Two routes, same answer.
<whisper>Part c leans on De Morgan.</whisper> Neither A nor B, A prime intersection B prime, is the complement of the union, so one minus zero point eight, which is zero point two.

Step back and see the shape, because the exam repeats it. The addition rule produces the union, then the complement of that union gives neither. Recognising this two step chain is worth more than any single formula.
<curious>एक staple J E E Main composition, एक setup तीन linked questions को feed करता है।</curious> दो events known probabilities और known overlap के साथ।
हमें बताया है P of A is zero point six, P of B is zero point five, और P of A intersection B is zero point three। Union, exactly one, और neither निकालो।
Part a, general addition rule: zero point six plus zero point five minus zero point three यानी zero point eight। वो है P of A union B।
Part b, exactly one overlap को दोनों तरफ़ से हटाता है, तो P of A plus P of B minus twice P of A intersection B, यानी zero point six plus zero point five minus zero point six, जो zero point five।
अच्छा cross check, exactly one बराबर है P of A union B minus P of A intersection B, zero point eight minus zero point three, फिर zero point five। दो रास्ते, एक ही answer।
Part c De Morgan पर टिकता है। Neither A nor B, A prime intersection B prime, union का complement है, तो one minus zero point eight, यानी zero point two।

<whisper>पीछे हटकर shape देखो, क्योंकि exam इसे दोहराता है।</whisper> Addition rule union देता है, फिर उस union का complement neither देता है। इस two step chain को पहचानना किसी single formula से ज़्यादा काम का है।

sections.title: Worked example: a die loaded by face value (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: Loaded die — axioms beat the counting formula (JEE Advanced)
$P(\text{face } k) \propto k$. Find each face's probability, then P(prime) and P(even OR > 4).
$n(A)/n(S)$ is WRONG here — outcomes aren't equally likely. Sum the sand instead.
Direct check: $E \cup G = \{2,4,5,6\}$, sand $= \tfrac{2+4+5+6}{21} = \tfrac{17}{21}$ ✓
