segments.text: Now the J E E Advanced case that the whole subtopic was built for, an experiment where the counting formula simply cannot work. A die is loaded so each face's probability is proportional to the number on it.
Proportional to the face value means P of face k equals c times k, for some constant c we need to find, then we want the probability of a prime, and of even or greater than four.
Normalization pins down c. The sand totals one, so c times one plus two up to six, that's twenty one c, equals one, giving c equals one over twenty one. So face k carries k over twenty one.

<whisper>Flag this loudly:</whisper> n of A over n of S would be flat wrong here, because the outcomes are not equally likely. This is precisely the case that breaks the classical recipe, so we sum the actual sand instead.
Primes on a die are two, three and five, so P of prime is their sand added, two plus three plus five over twenty one, which is ten over twenty one.

For even or greater than four, even is two, four, six and greater than four is five, six, overlapping at six. Addition rule: twelve over twenty one plus eleven over twenty one minus six over twenty one, which is seventeen over twenty one.

Check it directly, the union even or greater than four is the set two, four, five, six, whose sand is two plus four plus five plus six over twenty one, again seventeen over twenty one. The addition rule and the direct sum agree.
The bar chart shows it at a glance, the sand climbs with the face value, six carrying six times the sand of one. That slope is exactly why the equal likelihood formula had no business here.

अब वो J E E Advanced case जिसके लिए पूरा subtopic बना था, एक experiment जहाँ counting formula बिल्कुल काम नहीं कर सकता। एक die ऐसे loaded है कि हर face की probability उस पर लिखे number के proportional है।
Proportional to the face value का मतलब P of face k equals c into k, किसी constant c के लिए जो ढूंढना है, फिर हमें चाहिए probability of a prime, और of even or greater than four।
Normalization c को पकड़ लेता है। Sand का total one है, तो c into one plus two up to six, यानी twenty one c, equals one, जिससे c equals one over twenty one। तो face k रखता है k over twenty one।
इसे ज़ोर से flag करो: n of A over n of S यहाँ बिल्कुल गलत होगा, क्योंकि outcomes equally likely नहीं हैं। यही वो case है जो classical recipe को तोड़ता है, तो हम इसके बजाय actual sand जोड़ते हैं।
<whisper>Die पर primes हैं two, three और five,</whisper> तो P of prime इनकी sand जोड़ के है, two plus three plus five over twenty one, यानी ten over twenty one।

Even or greater than four के लिए, even है two, four, six और greater than four है five, six, six पर overlap करते हुए। Addition rule: twelve over twenty one plus eleven over twenty one minus six over twenty one, यानी seventeen over twenty one।

इसे directly check करो, union even or greater than four है set two, four, five, six, जिसकी sand है two plus four plus five plus six over twenty one, फिर seventeen over twenty one। Addition rule और direct sum agree करते हैं।
Bar chart इसे एक नज़र में दिखाता है, sand face value के साथ चढ़ती है, six one की छह गुना sand रखता है। वो slope ही बताता है कि equal likelihood formula का यहाँ कोई काम नहीं था।

sections.subtopic: Probability of Events and the Axiomatic Approach
sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Pitfalls & Pro-Tips
1. Applying $n(A)/n(S)$ to a loaded/unfair experiment. It's a consequence of equal likelihood, not a definition.
2. Forgetting to subtract the overlap. Only drop $-P(A \cap B)$ once you've checked A, B are mutually exclusive.
3. Treating mutually exclusive as independent. ME: $P(A \cap B)=0$. Independent: $P(A \cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
4. A probability outside $[0,1]$ means an arithmetic error — full stop. Use the range as a free check.
Pro-Tip: see "at least one" → reach for the complement. $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})$.
It turns a messy union into a single easy count — the highest-leverage one-liner in the chapter.

segments.text: Let's close with the four mistakes that quietly drain marks in this subtopic, and the one reflex worth drilling.

Pitfall one, applying n of A over n of S to a loaded or unfair experiment. That formula is a consequence of equal likelihood, not a definition. For a biased coin or a die loaded by face value, go back to the axioms and sum the actual sand.

Pitfall two, forgetting to subtract the overlap. Writing P of A union B as just P of A plus P of B, when A and B overlap, double counts the intersection. Only drop the minus P of A intersection B term after you've checked the events are mutually exclusive.

Pitfall three, the big one, treating mutually exclusive as independent. For mutually exclusive events P of A intersection B is zero. For independent events it's P of A times P of B. These are different ideas, so never multiply probabilities in a Class eleven addition rule problem.
Pitfall four is a free gift, if your answer is negative or bigger than one, you've made an arithmetic slip, full stop. Use the zero to one range as an automatic sanity check on every final number.
<whisper>And the pro tip that outclasses everything else in this chapter:</whisper> the moment you see at least one, reach for the complement. P of at least one equals one minus P of none.
It almost always turns a messy union of many cases into a single, clean count of the none case. Train that reflex now, it's the highest leverage one liner in the whole chapter.
<curious>चलो इस subtopic की चार mistakes के साथ close करें जो चुपचाप marks सोख लेती हैं, और वो एक reflex जो drill करने लायक है।</curious>

Pitfall one, n of A over n of S को loaded या unfair experiment पर लगाना। वो formula equal likelihood का consequence है, definition नहीं। Biased coin या face value से loaded die के लिए, axioms पर वापस जाओ और actual sand जोड़ो।

Pitfall two, overlap subtract करना भूल जाना। P of A union B को बस P of A plus P of B लिखना, जब A और B overlap करें, intersection को double count करता है। Minus P of A intersection B term तभी हटाओ जब check कर लो events mutually exclusive हैं।

Pitfall three, बड़ी वाली, mutually exclusive को independent समझना। Mutually exclusive events के लिए P of A intersection B zero है। Independent events के लिए वो P of A into P of B है। ये अलग ideas हैं, तो Class eleven addition rule problem में probabilities कभी multiply मत करो।
Pitfall four एक मुफ़्त तोहफ़ा है, अगर आपका answer negative या one से बड़ा है, तो arithmetic slip हुई है, बस। Zero से one range को हर final number पर automatic sanity check की तरह use करो।
और वो pro tip जो इस chapter में बाक़ी सबको पीछे छोड़ देती है: जैसे ही at least one दिखे, complement की तरफ़ जाओ। P of at least one equals one minus P of none।
<whisper>यह लगभग हमेशा कई cases के messy union को none case के एक साफ़ count में बदल देती है।</whisper> वो reflex अभी train करो, यह पूरे chapter की highest leverage one liner है।

sections.subtopic: Computing Probabilities: Combinatorial Methods, Multi-Event Addition and Odds
sections.title: Computing P(E) by counting: order or no order

board_events.text: Computing P(E) when you can't list every outcome
For equally likely outcomes, $P(E)=\dfrac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ still holds — the work moves to COUNTING.
Too many outcomes to list → count with permutations and combinations.
First question, always: does ORDER matter? Arrangements → nPr. Selections → nCr.
Count $n(E)$ and $n(S)$ by the SAME method — both ordered, or both unordered.

segments.text: <curious>The axioms subtopic gave us the rules of probability. This subtopic is about actually computing it when the sample space is too big to write out.</curious> The formula doesn't change, the challenge moves.
For equally likely outcomes, P of E still equals n of E over n of S. Nothing new there. What's new is that both counts can be huge, so the real work becomes counting cleverly.
When there are hundreds or thousands of outcomes, you don't list them, you count them with permutations and combinations from the counting chapter.
If order matters, you use permutations, n P r, which is n factorial over n minus r factorial. Arrangements, rankings, seat orders, all order sensitive.
If order does not matter, you use combinations, n C r, which divides further by r factorial to cancel the rearrangements. Committees, hands of cards, selections.
So the very first question on any counting probability, before touching a formula, is does order matter? Arrangements point to n P r, selections point to n C r.
And one discipline that saves marks, count n of E and n of S the same way. If the numerator counts ordered, the denominator must too, otherwise the ratio is meaningless.
पिछले subtopic ने probability के rules दिए। यह subtopic उसे actually compute करने के बारे में है जब sample space इतना बड़ा हो कि लिखा न जा सके। Formula नहीं बदलता, challenge shift होती है।
<curious>Equally likely outcomes के लिए P of E अब भी equals n of E over n of S. कुछ नया नहीं।</curious> नया यह है कि दोनों counts बहुत बड़े हो सकते हैं, तो असली काम cleverly counting बन जाता है।
जब सैकड़ों या हज़ारों outcomes हों, आप उन्हें list नहीं करते, permutations और combinations से count करते हो, counting chapter से।
अगर order matters, permutations use करो, n P r, जो है n factorial over n minus r factorial। Arrangements, rankings, seat orders, सब order sensitive।
अगर order matter नहीं करता, combinations use करो, n C r, जो r factorial से और divide करता है ताकि rearrangements cancel हों। Committees, cards के hands, selections।
तो किसी भी counting probability पर पहला सवाल, formula छूने से पहले, यही, does order matter? Arrangements n P r की तरफ़, selections n C r की तरफ़।
और एक discipline जो marks बचाती है, n of E और n of S को एक ही तरीक़े से count करो। अगर numerator ordered गिनता है, denominator को भी ordered गिनना होगा, वरना ratio meaningless है।

sections.title: The "at least one" strategy

board_events.text: The "at least one" strategy
"At least one" spans many messy cases — exactly one, exactly two, ... all the way up.
Its complement is a SINGLE clean case: "none."
Example: at least one head in 5 tosses → "none" = all tails.
Trigger phrase: read "at least one" → compute the "none" case and subtract from 1.

board_events.caption: P(at least one) fills everything except the single 'none' slice
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 420 120" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="210" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#333">Total probability = 1</text><rect x="40" y="46" width="58" height="32" fill="#a9d6c4" stroke="#2a8c6a" stroke-width="1.5"/><rect x="98" y="46" width="282" height="32" fill="#ffd9a0" stroke="#c8862a" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="69" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#2a7d5f">P(none)</text><text x="239" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11.5" fill="#8a5a12">P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)</text></svg>

segments.text: Here's the highest value tactic in the whole computing toolkit, and it hangs on the complement law from the axioms subtopic.
The phrase at least one hides a mess. At least one success could mean exactly one, or exactly two, all the way up to all of them. Adding those cases directly is painful.
<excited>But its complement is a single, clean case, none.</excited> Exactly zero successes. One case instead of many.
So P of at least one equals one minus P of none. You trade a long sum for one short subtraction.
Take at least one head in five coin tosses. The none case is all five tails, delightfully simple.
P of all tails is one half to the fifth, which is one over thirty two, so P of at least one head is one minus that, thirty one over thirty two.
Lock in the trigger. The instant you read at least one, don't enumerate. Compute the none case and subtract it from one.
The bar makes it vivid, the whole probability is one, the none case is one thin slice, and at least one is the entire rest of the bar. You compute the thin slice and keep the rest.
<excited>यह पूरे computing toolkit की highest value tactic है, और यह axioms subtopic के complement law पर टिकी है।</excited>
Phrase at least one एक mess छिपाती है। At least one success का मतलब exactly one, या exactly two, ऊपर all of them तक। इन cases को सीधे जोड़ना painful है।
पर इसका complement एक single, clean case है, none। Exactly zero successes। कई के बजाय एक case।
तो P of at least one equals one minus P of none। आप एक लंबे sum को एक छोटी subtraction से बदल देते हो।
Five coin tosses में at least one head लो। None case है सारे five tails, बड़ा ही simple।
P of all tails है one half to the fifth, यानी one over thirty two, तो P of at least one head है one minus that, thirty one over thirty two।
Trigger fix कर लो। जैसे ही at least one पढ़ो, enumerate मत करो। None case compute करो और one से subtract कर दो।
Bar इसे vivid कर देता है, पूरी probability one है, none case एक पतली slice है, और at least one बाक़ी पूरा bar। आप पतली slice compute करते हो और बाक़ी रख लेते हो।

sections.title: More than two events: inclusion–exclusion

board_events.text: More than two events: inclusion–exclusion
Two events double-count the overlap once. Three events double-count worse.

board_events.latex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
P(A\cup B\cup C) = P(A)+P(B)+P(C) - P(A\cap B) - P(B\cap C) - P(A\cap C) + P(A\cap B\cap C)

board_events.text: Pattern: add singles, subtract pairs, add back the triple — alternating signs.
The same pieces answer "exactly one" and "neither" too.

board_events.caption: Three circles: add singles, subtract pairs, add back the centre
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 360 345" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="135" cy="135" r="80" fill="#ffd9a0" fill-opacity="0.45" stroke="#c8862a" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="225" cy="135" r="80" fill="#a9d6c4" fill-opacity="0.45" stroke="#2a8c6a" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="180" cy="218" r="80" fill="#c9b3e0" fill-opacity="0.45" stroke="#7a5ba6" stroke-width="2"/><text x="90" y="98" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#8a5a12">A</text><text x="270" y="98" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#2a7d5f">B</text><text x="180" y="300" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#5a3f80">C</text><text x="180" y="163" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#555">A∩B∩C</text><text x="180" y="333" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11.5" fill="#333">+ singles − pairs + (A∩B∩C)</text></svg>

segments.text: When three events overlap, the addition rule grows, but it grows in a beautifully regular pattern called inclusion exclusion.
Recall the two event case, adding P of A and P of B counts the overlap twice, so you subtract it once. With three events the over counting is worse, and there's a triple overlap to worry about too.
Two events, one correction: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A intersection B.
<curious>Three events, watch the rhythm.</curious> Add the three singles, subtract all three pairwise intersections, then add back the one triple intersection.
That's the whole pattern, add singles, subtract pairs, add back the triple. The signs alternate, which is exactly why it's called inclusion exclusion.
The same building blocks answer neighbouring questions too, like exactly one of A and B, or neither of them, without any new machinery.
Exactly one of A and B is P of A plus P of B minus twice P of A intersection B, you strip the overlap from both sides instead of once.

The three circle picture shows why. The pairwise lenses each get counted twice by the singles, so you subtract them, but then the very centre, A intersection B intersection C, has been subtracted one time too many, so you add it back once.
<curious>जब तीन events overlap करें, addition rule बढ़ता है, पर एक ख़ूबसूरत regular pattern में, जिसे inclusion exclusion कहते हैं।</curious>
Two event case याद करो, P of A और P of B जोड़ने से overlap दो बार गिना जाता है, तो एक बार subtract करते हो। तीन events के साथ over counting और बुरी होती है, और एक triple overlap की भी चिंता है।
Two events, one correction: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A intersection B।
Three events, rhythm देखो। तीन singles जोड़ो, तीनों pairwise intersections subtract करो, फिर एक triple intersection add back करो।
यही पूरा pattern है, singles जोड़ो, pairs घटाओ, triple add back करो। Signs alternate करते हैं, इसीलिए इसे inclusion exclusion कहते हैं।
वही building blocks पड़ोसी सवालों के जवाब भी देते हैं, जैसे exactly one of A and B, या neither, बिना किसी नई machinery के।
Exactly one of A and B है P of A plus P of B minus twice P of A intersection B, आप overlap को एक के बजाय दोनों तरफ़ से हटाते हो।

तीन circle picture बताती है क्यों। हर pairwise lens singles से दो बार गिना जाता है, तो उन्हें subtract करते हो, पर फिर बीच वाला, A intersection B intersection C, एक बार ज़्यादा subtract हो गया, तो उसे एक बार add back करते हो।

sections.title: Two more languages for chance: odds and empirical

board_events.text: Two more languages for chance: odds & empirical
ODDS compare favourable to unfavourable, not favourable to total.

board_events.latex: \text{odds against} = n : m \;\Rightarrow\; P = \dfrac{m}{m+n}\ (\text{favourable still } m)

board_events.text: Odds split the SAME whole: $m : n$ are the TWO PARTS; the denominator is $m+n$, not $n$.
EMPIRICAL (experimental) probability: no theory, just observed frequency.
As trials grow large, empirical probability settles toward the classical value (law of large numbers, informal).

segments.text: Two more ways to talk about chance show up in exams, odds and empirical probability. Both are easy once you see how they relate to what you already know.
<whisper>Odds are a favourite trap</whisper> because they compare favourable to unfavourable outcomes, not favourable to total. That one shift causes most odds mistakes.
If the odds in favour are m to n, then the probability is m over m plus n. The m and n are the two parts, and their sum is the whole.
Odds against of n to m describe the same situation, the favourable count is still m, so the probability is still m over m plus n.
So the key is, odds split the same whole into two parts, m and n. The denominator of the probability is m plus n, never just n. Get that and odds stop being scary.
Empirical, or experimental, probability throws out theory entirely. You just run the experiment many times and record what actually happened.
P of E is approximately the number of times E occurred over the total number of trials, a plain observed frequency.
And here's the bridge, as the number of trials grows large, that empirical fraction settles toward the classical probability. That's the law of large numbers, stated informally.
<curious>Exams में chance के बारे में बात करने के दो और तरीक़े आते हैं, odds और empirical probability.</curious> दोनों आसान हैं जब देख लो कि ये जो पहले से पता है उससे कैसे जुड़ते हैं।
Odds एक favourite trap हैं क्योंकि ये favourable को unfavourable से compare करते हैं, favourable को total से नहीं। वही एक shift ज़्यादातर odds mistakes की वजह है।
अगर odds in favour m to n हैं, तो probability है m over m plus n। m और n दो parts हैं, और इनका sum पूरा whole।
Odds against of n to m वही situation बताते हैं, favourable count अब भी m है, तो probability अब भी m over m plus n।
<whisper>तो key यह है, odds उसी whole को दो parts में बाँटते हैं, m और n।</whisper> Probability का denominator m plus n है, कभी सिर्फ़ n नहीं। यह समझ लो तो odds डरावने नहीं रहते।
Empirical, या experimental, probability theory को पूरी तरह छोड़ देती है। आप बस experiment कई बार चलाते हो और record करते हो कि actually क्या हुआ।
P of E लगभग है number of times E occurred over total number of trials, एक plain observed frequency।
और यह रहा bridge, जैसे-जैसे trials की संख्या बड़ी होती है, वो empirical fraction classical probability की तरफ़ settle हो जाती है। यही law of large numbers है, informally कहा गया।

sections.title: Computing toolkit — counting, complement, addition

board_events.text: Computing toolkit — part 1

board_events.latex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
P(A\cup B\cup C) = \textstyle\sum P(\text{single}) - \sum P(\text{pair}) + P(A\cap B\cap C)

board_events.text: Every line needs equally likely outcomes OR given probabilities — never mix a count with a raw probability.

segments.text: <curious>Let's lay out the computing formulas in one place, the ones you'll reach for in the computing problems.</curious>
The counting probability: P of E equals n of E over n of S, where both counts come from permutations or combinations, whichever the order question demands.
The at least one shortcut: P of at least one equals one minus P of none. Highest leverage line in the section.
The complement law it rests on: P of A prime equals one minus P of A.
The two event addition rule: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A intersection B.
The three event version: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add back the triple intersection.
And exactly one of A and B, P of A plus P of B minus twice P of A intersection B.

<whisper>One consistency rule ties them together.</whisper> Every line needs either equally likely outcomes or probabilities you've been given. Never mix a raw count with a probability in the same expression.
Computing formulas को एक जगह रख लें, वो जो computing problems में काम आएँगे।
Counting probability: P of E equals n of E over n of S, जहाँ दोनों counts permutations या combinations से आते हैं, जो order का सवाल माँगे।
<excited>At least one shortcut: P of at least one equals one minus P of none।</excited> Section की highest leverage line।
जिस complement law पर यह टिकी है: P of A prime equals one minus P of A।
Two event addition rule: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A intersection B।
Three event version: singles जोड़ो, pairs घटाओ, triple intersection add back करो।
और exactly one of A and B, P of A plus P of B minus twice P of A intersection B।
एक consistency rule इन्हें बाँधता है। हर line को या तो equally likely outcomes चाहिए या given probabilities। एक ही expression में raw count और probability कभी mix मत करो।

sections.title: Computing toolkit — odds and empirical

board_events.text: Computing toolkit — part 2: odds & empirical
$P_{\text{empirical}} \to P_{\text{classical}}$ as $N \to \infty$ (law of large numbers, informal).
Odds → probability: sum the two parts for the denominator. Probability → odds: it's $P : (1-P)$.

segments.text: <curious>Now the odds and empirical formulas, plus the conversions that trip people up.</curious>
Odds in favour of m to n give probability m over m plus n. The favourable part on top, the whole on the bottom.
Odds against of n to m describe the same experiment, so E still has probability m over m plus n, and its complement n over m plus n.
Going the other way, from a probability to odds, the ratio is P of E to one minus P of E. Probability of success against probability of failure.
Empirical probability is frequency over trials, f over N, straight from the data with no theory.
As N grows without bound, that empirical value converges to the classical probability, the informal law of large numbers.
Hold the two conversions. Odds to probability, sum the two parts for the denominator. Probability to odds, it's P to one minus P. Mixing these up is the classic odds error.
अब odds और empirical formulas, साथ में वो conversions जो लोगों को गिराती हैं।
<curious>Odds in favour of m to n देते हैं probability m over m plus n।</curious> Favourable part ऊपर, पूरा whole नीचे।
Odds against of n to m वही experiment बताते हैं, तो E की probability अब भी m over m plus n, और उसके complement की n over m plus n।
उल्टी तरफ़, probability से odds, ratio है P of E to one minus P of E। Probability of success against probability of failure।
Empirical probability है frequency over trials, f over N, सीधे data से बिना किसी theory के।
जैसे N बिना सीमा बढ़े, वो empirical value classical probability की तरफ़ converge करती है, informal law of large numbers।
दो conversions पकड़ लो। Odds से probability, denominator के लिए दोनों parts जोड़ो। Probability से odds, वो है P to one minus P। इन्हें उलट देना ही classic odds error है।

sections.title: Worked example: forming a committee (CBSE)

board_events.text: Worked Example — committee selection (CBSE)
From 5 men and 4 women, a committee of 3 is chosen at random. Find P(exactly 2 women).
Selection, order irrelevant → use combinations throughout.
Both counts are combinations — consistent, so the ratio is valid.

segments.text: <curious>A standard C B S E counting problem, three marks, that lives entirely on choosing the right count.</curious>
From five men and four women, we pick a committee of three at random, and we want the probability of exactly two women.
First question, does order matter? A committee is a selection, the seating is irrelevant, so everything here is combinations, not permutations.
The sample space is all ways to choose three people from nine, nine C three, which is nine factorial over three factorial six factorial, equal to eighty four.
For the event, exactly two women means choose two of the four women and one of the five men, four C two times five C one, six times five, which is thirty.
So the probability is thirty over eighty four, and reducing gives five over fourteen.

<whisper>Notice the consistency.</whisper> Both the numerator and denominator were counted as combinations, so the ratio is meaningful. Mixing a permutation count on top with a combination count below would silently corrupt the answer.
एक standard C B S E counting problem, तीन marks का, जो पूरी तरह सही count चुनने पर टिका है।
पाँच men और चार women में से, हम random एक committee of three चुनते हैं, और हमें चाहिए probability of exactly two women।
<curious>पहला सवाल, does order matter?</curious> Committee एक selection है, seating irrelevant, तो यहाँ सब combinations है, permutations नहीं।
Sample space है nine में से three चुनने के सारे तरीक़े, nine C three, जो nine factorial over three factorial six factorial, बराबर eighty four।
Event के लिए, exactly two women का मतलब four women में से two और five men में से one चुनो, four C two times five C one, six into five, यानी thirty।
तो probability है thirty over eighty four, और reduce करने पर five over fourteen।
Consistency देखो। Numerator और denominator दोनों combinations से गिने गए, तो ratio meaningful है। ऊपर permutation count और नीचे combination count mix करना चुपके से answer बिगाड़ देता।

sections.subtopic: Computing Probabilities: Combinatorial Methods, Multi-Event Addition and Odds
sections.title: Worked example: at least one defective (JEE Main)

board_events.text: "At least one" in action (JEE Main)
A box has 12 bulbs, 3 defective. 4 are drawn at random (without replacement). Find P(at least one defective).
"At least one" → complement. Compute P(none defective) = P(all 4 good).
Direct route would need P(exactly 1)+P(exactly 2)+P(exactly 3) — three terms.
One subtraction replaced a three-term sum — that's the whole point of the complement trick.

segments.text: Now the at least one trigger in a real J E E Main setting, drawing bulbs from a box.
A box has twelve bulbs, three of them defective. We draw four at random without replacement, and we want the probability of at least one defective.
<excited>The phrase at least one fires the complement reflex.</excited> Instead of that, compute P of none defective, which means all four drawn are good.
The good bulbs number nine, so P of none defective is nine C four over twelve C four, that's one hundred twenty six over four hundred ninety five, which reduces to fourteen over fifty five.
Then subtract from one. P of at least one defective is one minus fourteen over fifty five, which is forty one over fifty five.
Compare the direct route, you'd need P of exactly one plus P of exactly two plus P of exactly three defective, three separate combination terms, each fiddly.
<whisper>One clean subtraction replaced a three term sum.</whisper> That contrast is exactly why the complement trick is worth drilling until it's automatic.
<excited>अब at least one trigger एक असली J E E Main setting में, box से bulbs निकालना।</excited>
एक box में बारह bulbs हैं, उनमें से three defective। हम random चार निकालते हैं without replacement, और हमें चाहिए probability of at least one defective।
Phrase at least one complement reflex चला देती है। उसके बजाय P of none defective compute करो, यानी चारों drawn अच्छे हों।
अच्छे bulbs हैं nine, तो P of none defective है nine C four over twelve C four, यानी one hundred twenty six over four hundred ninety five, जो reduce होकर fourteen over fifty five।
फिर one से subtract करो। P of at least one defective है one minus fourteen over fifty five, यानी forty one over fifty five।
Direct route से compare करो, आपको चाहिए होता P of exactly one plus P of exactly two plus P of exactly three defective, तीन अलग combination terms, हर एक fiddly।
एक clean subtraction ने तीन-term sum को replace कर दिया। यही contrast बताता है कि complement trick को तब तक drill करने लायक है जब तक automatic न हो जाए।

sections.title: Worked example: three-event inclusion–exclusion (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Three-event inclusion–exclusion (JEE Main)
P(M)=0.5, P(P)=0.4, P(C)=0.3; pairwise 0.2, 0.15, 0.1; all three 0.05. Find P(at least one subject).
P(none of the three) = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2 — the complement, instantly.

segments.text: <curious>The three event addition rule shows up constantly in J E E Main, usually dressed as students taking subjects.</curious>

In a class, the probability a student takes Maths is zero point five, Physics zero point four, Chemistry zero point three. The pairwise overlaps are zero point two, zero point one five and zero point one, and all three together zero point zero five. Find the probability of at least one subject.
Apply inclusion exclusion, add the singles, subtract the pairs, add back the triple.
Plug in: the singles are zero point five plus zero point four plus zero point three, the pairs are zero point two plus zero point one five plus zero point one, and the triple is zero point zero five.
That's one point two minus zero point four five plus zero point zero five, which comes to zero point eight.
<curious>And a free bonus from the complement.</curious> The probability of none of the three subjects is one minus zero point eight, which is zero point two, no extra work.
The three circle diagram is the whole justification, the singles over count the pairwise lenses, so you subtract them, and the centre gets subtracted once too often, so you add it back.
Three event addition rule J E E Main में लगातार आता है, आमतौर पर students के subjects लेने के रूप में।

<curious>एक class में, probability कि student Maths लेता है zero point five, Physics zero point four, Chemistry zero point three।</curious> Pairwise overlaps हैं zero point two, zero point one five और zero point one, और तीनों साथ zero point zero five। Probability of at least one subject निकालो।
Inclusion exclusion लगाओ, singles जोड़ो, pairs घटाओ, triple add back करो।
Plug in करो: singles हैं zero point five plus zero point four plus zero point three, pairs हैं zero point two plus zero point one five plus zero point one, और triple है zero point zero five।
यह है one point two minus zero point four five plus zero point zero five, जो आता है zero point eight।
और complement से एक free bonus। Probability of none of the three subjects है one minus zero point eight, यानी zero point two, कोई extra काम नहीं।
तीन circle diagram पूरा justification है, singles pairwise lenses को over count करते हैं, तो उन्हें subtract करते हो, और centre एक बार ज़्यादा subtract हो जाता है, तो उसे add back करते हो।

sections.title: Worked example: odds and empirical probability (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: Odds meets empirical (JEE Advanced flavour)
(a) The odds against a team winning are 4 : 3. Find P(win).
(b) In 200 trials an event occurred 130 times. Give empirical P and the odds in favour.

board_events.caption: Odds 3 : 4 split the whole of 7 parts — P(win) = 3/7

board_events.text: Trap: for odds AGAINST 4 : 3, the 3 is favourable and the denominator is 4+3, not 4.

segments.text: <curious>This closes the subtopic by fusing odds and empirical probability, exactly the blend J E E Advanced likes.</curious>
Part a, the odds against a team winning are four to three. Find the probability the team wins.

Odds against of four to three means three favourable parts and four unfavourable, so P of win is three over four plus three, which is three sevenths. The direction word against is doing the work, so read it slowly.
Part b switches to data. In two hundred trials an event occurred one hundred thirty times. Give the empirical probability and the odds in favour.
Empirical probability is frequency over trials, one hundred thirty over two hundred, which reduces to thirteen over twenty.
For odds in favour, take P to one minus P, thirteen over twenty against seven over twenty, which is thirteen to seven.
The split bar shows part a cleanly, the whole is seven equal parts, three favour the win and four don't, so the win probability is three of the seven.

<whisper>And the trap to circle in red:</whisper> for odds against four to three, the favourable count is the three, and the denominator is four plus three, never just the four. Misreading the direction is the single most common odds mistake.
यह subtopic को odds और empirical probability जोड़कर close करता है, बिल्कुल वो blend जो J E E Advanced को पसंद है।
<curious>Part a, किसी team के जीतने के odds against four to three हैं।</curious> Probability निकालो कि team जीते।

Odds against of four to three का मतलब three favourable parts और four unfavourable, तो P of win है three over four plus three, यानी three sevenths। Direction word against काम कर रहा है, तो इसे धीरे पढ़ो।
Part b data पर switch करता है। दो सौ trials में एक event एक सौ तीस बार occur हुआ। Empirical probability और odds in favour दो।
Empirical probability है frequency over trials, one hundred thirty over two hundred, जो reduce होकर thirteen over twenty।
Odds in favour के लिए, P to one minus P लो, thirteen over twenty against seven over twenty, यानी thirteen to seven।
Split bar part a को साफ़ दिखाता है, पूरा whole seven equal parts है, तीन win के favour में और चार नहीं, तो win probability है seven में से three।
और red में घेरने वाला trap: odds against four to three के लिए, favourable count है three, और denominator है four plus three, कभी सिर्फ़ four नहीं। Direction गलत पढ़ना ही सबसे common odds mistake है।

sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Pitfalls & Pro-Tips
1. Mixing ordered and unordered counts. Count $n(E)$ and $n(S)$ by the SAME method.
2. Odds ≠ probability. Odds $m:n \to$ probability $m/(m+n)$, NOT $m/n$.
3. Forgetting the +triple in three-event inclusion–exclusion (or a sign error).
4. Enumerating "at least one" case-by-case instead of using the complement.
Pro-Tip: read for order FIRST, then for the trigger "at least" — two reflexes solve most of this.
The counting decision (nPr vs nCr) and the complement reflex cover the bulk of the marks.

segments.text: <curious>Let's close this subtopic with the four mistakes that cost the most, and two reflexes that prevent them.</curious>
Pitfall one, mixing ordered and unordered counts. If you count n of E with combinations, you must count n of S with combinations too. Consistency top and bottom is non negotiable.
Pitfall two, treating odds as probability. Odds of m to n give probability m over m plus n, not m over n. The denominator is the sum of both parts.
Pitfall three, in three event inclusion exclusion, forgetting to add back the triple intersection, or flipping a sign. Write the pattern out, add singles, subtract pairs, add the triple, every time.
Pitfall four, grinding through at least one case by case, exactly one, exactly two, and so on, when the complement collapses it to one minus P of none.

<whisper>Two reflexes cover most of this subtopic.</whisper> First, read the question for order before choosing a counting formula. Second, scan for the trigger word at least and switch to the complement.
Get the counting decision right, n P r versus n C r, and make the complement automatic, and you've secured the bulk of this subtopic's marks with almost no wasted effort.
इस subtopic को उन चार mistakes के साथ close करें जो सबसे ज़्यादा महँगी हैं, और दो reflexes जो इन्हें रोकते हैं।
<curious>Pitfall one, ordered और unordered counts mix करना।</curious> अगर n of E combinations से गिनते हो, तो n of S भी combinations से गिनना होगा। ऊपर-नीचे consistency non negotiable है।
Pitfall two, odds को probability समझना। Odds of m to n देते हैं probability m over m plus n, m over n नहीं। Denominator दोनों parts का sum है।
Pitfall three, three event inclusion exclusion में, triple intersection add back करना भूलना, या sign flip कर देना। Pattern लिख लो, singles जोड़ो, pairs घटाओ, triple जोड़ो, हर बार।
Pitfall four, at least one को case by case पीसना, exactly one, exactly two, वगैरह, जब complement इसे one minus P of none में समेट देता है।
दो reflexes इस subtopic का ज़्यादातर हिस्सा cover करते हैं। पहला, counting formula चुनने से पहले question में order पढ़ो। दूसरा, trigger word at least scan करो और complement पर switch करो।
<whisper>Counting decision सही करो, n P r versus n C r, और complement को automatic बना दो,</whisper> और आपने इस subtopic के ज़्यादातर marks लगभग बिना किसी बर्बाद मेहनत के secure कर लिए।

board_events.text: Formula Recap — foundations

board_events.latex: n(S) = m_1 \times m_2 \times \cdots \times m_k \quad (k \text{ independent stages})
\text{Axioms: } P(A)\ge 0;\ P(S)=1;\ A\cap B=\varnothing \Rightarrow P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)

segments.text: <curious>Time to consolidate the whole chapter's formulas, starting with the foundations from the first two subtopics.</curious>
Sample space size for independent stages is the product of the per stage counts, m one times m two, up to m k.
The event counts, a space of n outcomes has two to the power n events in total, and two to the power n minus n minus one of them are compound.
The three relationships, mutually exclusive is empty intersection, exhaustive is union equal to S, and a partition needs both at once.
The three axioms, non negativity, normalization, and additivity for mutually exclusive events. Everything in the second subtopic came from these.
The immediate consequences, the impossible event is zero, probabilities lie between zero and one, and the complement law.
And the formula everyone overuses, P of A equals n of A over n of S, valid only when outcomes are equally likely.
पूरे chapter के formulas consolidate करने का समय, पहले दो subtopics की foundations से शुरू।
<curious>Independent stages के लिए sample space size per stage counts का product है, m one times m two, m k तक।</curious>
Event counts, n outcomes वाले space में total two to the power n events, और उनमें से two to the power n minus n minus one compound।
तीन relationships, mutually exclusive यानी empty intersection, exhaustive यानी union equal to S, और partition को दोनों एक साथ चाहिए।
तीन axioms, non negativity, normalization, और mutually exclusive events के लिए additivity। दूसरे subtopic का सब कुछ इन्हीं से आया।
तुरंत मिलने वाले consequences, impossible event zero है, probabilities zero और one के बीच, और complement law।
और वो formula जिसे सब overuse करते हैं, P of A equals n of A over n of S, valid सिर्फ़ तब जब outcomes equally likely हों।

board_events.text: Formula Recap — addition, computing, odds

board_events.latex: P(A\cup B\cup C) = \textstyle\sum\text{singles} - \sum\text{pairs} + P(A\cap B\cap C)
P(\text{exactly one})=P(A)+P(B)-2P(A\cap B);\quad P(A'\cap B')=1-P(A\cup B)

segments.text: Now the addition family, the computing tools, and the odds and empirical formulas.
The two event addition rule, P of A union B is P of A plus P of B minus the overlap.
The three event version, add singles, subtract pairs, add back the triple intersection.
The two handy identities, exactly one of A and B, and neither, both built from the same pieces by De Morgan.
The at least one shortcut, one minus P of none, the highest leverage line in the chapter.
The counting choice, permutations n P r when order matters, combinations n C r when it doesn't.
<curious>And finally, odds and empirical,</curious> odds m to n give m over m plus n, and empirical probability is frequency over trials.
अब addition family, computing tools, और odds व empirical formulas।
Two event addition rule, P of A union B है P of A plus P of B minus overlap।
Three event version, singles जोड़ो, pairs घटाओ, triple intersection add back करो।
<curious>दो handy identities, exactly one of A and B, और neither, दोनों उन्हीं pieces से De Morgan द्वारा बने।</curious>
At least one shortcut, one minus P of none, chapter की highest leverage line।
Counting choice, order matter करे तो permutations n P r, न करे तो combinations n C r।
और आख़िर में, odds और empirical, odds m to n देते हैं m over m plus n, और empirical probability है frequency over trials।

sections.title: Cheat sheet — quick recall (foundations)

board_events.text: Cheat Sheet — quick recall (foundations)
Event = subset of S. Outcome = one point. "or" → ∪, "and" → ∩.
$n$ outcomes → $n$ simple events, $2^n$ total events.
ME: $A\cap B=\varnothing$. Exhaustive: $\cup = S$. Partition = both.
Axioms in one breath: $P\ge 0$; $P(S)=1$; disjoint add.
Complement $P(A')=1-P(A)$ — your first move on "at least" and "not."
Sanity: every probability must land in $[0,1]$. Outside → error.

segments.text: <excited>Here's the rapid recall card for the foundations, the things you should be able to fire off without thinking.</excited>
An event is a subset of S, an outcome is a single point, and translate the English first, or means union, and means intersection.
A space of n outcomes has n simple events and two to the power n events in total.
Mutually exclusive is empty intersection, exhaustive is union equal to S, and a partition is both together.
The axioms in one breath, probability is non negative, the whole space has probability one, and disjoint events add.
<excited>The complement law, P of A prime equals one minus P of A,</excited> is your first move whenever you see at least or not.
And the free sanity check, every probability must land between zero and one. Anything outside means you slipped.
यह रहा foundations का rapid recall card, वो चीज़ें जो बिना सोचे fire करनी आनी चाहिए।
Event S का subset है, outcome एक single point, और पहले English translate करो, or यानी union, and यानी intersection।
n outcomes वाले space में n simple events और total two to the power n events।
Mutually exclusive यानी empty intersection, exhaustive यानी union equal to S, और partition दोनों साथ।
<excited>Axioms एक साँस में, probability non negative, पूरे space की probability one, और disjoint events जुड़ते हैं।</excited>
Complement law, P of A prime equals one minus P of A, आपकी पहली चाल है जब भी at least या not दिखे।
और free sanity check, हर probability zero और one के बीच होनी चाहिए। बाहर कुछ भी मतलब गड़बड़ हुई।

sections.title: Cheat sheet — which tool when (computing)

board_events.text: Cheat Sheet — which tool when (computing)
Equally likely? YES → $n(E)/n(S)$. NO → sum sand / use given probabilities.
